chapters.title: Rotational Mechanics
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the rotational motion of rigid bodies about a fixed axis, using everyday examples like a pulley at a well. It distinguishes rotational motion from translational motion and explains why a body can have zero net force yet still not be in rotational equilibrium.
key_concepts: Rotation of a rigid body about a fixed line

book_skeleton.subject_overview: This textbook covers rotational mechanics, focusing on the motion of rigid bodies rotating about a fixed axis. It explores how forces and torques produce angular acceleration and examines conditions of rotational equilibrium.

chapters.title: Rotational Mechanics
chapters.summary: This chapter introduces the rotational motion of rigid bodies about a fixed axis, using everyday examples like a pulley at a well. It distinguishes rotational motion from translational motion and explains why a body can have zero net force yet still not be in rotational equilibrium.

events.text: Centre of each circle = foot of perpendicular to the axis
Radius = distance from axis
Each particle: centre on axis, same time per turn
Same angle, same time — that's why we measure rotation by angle
Every particle sweeps the same angle theta
theta measured in radians, full turn = two pi
Q: Motor at 100 rev/min comes to rest in 15 s under constant deceleration. Find revolutions made.
omega_0 = 10pi/3 rad/s, omega = 0, t = 15 s
theta = 25pi rad = 12.5 revolutions
Q: Fan from rest reaches 400 rpm in 5 s (constant angular acceleration). Find time to reach 200 rpm.
400 rev/min = 0 + alpha x 5 s   ... (i)
200 rev/min = 0 + alpha x t   ... (ii)
t = 2.5 seconds
Q: Pulley radius 10 cm, rope does not slip. Bucket speed 20 cm/s, acceleration 4.0 m/s2. Find pulley's omega and alpha.
omega = v / r = (20 cm/s) / (10 cm) = 2 rad/s
alpha = a / r = (4.0 m/s2) / (10 cm) = 40 rad/s2
omega = 2 rad/s, alpha = 40 rad/s2
omega = d theta / d t, one number for the whole body
spin speeding up = angular acceleration
Angular acceleration possible even with zero net force
No angular acceleration without an external force
torque = the twisting effect of a force
torque = turning effect of a force
Torque is r crossed with F
Equilibrium needs BOTH: zero net force AND zero net torque
Sum Fx = 0, Sum Fy = 0
Coplanar forces: take torque about ANY point and still get zero
Friction at the tyres supplies the inward force
Lean inward so friction can curve your path
Weight times horizontal offset equals inward force times height
Q: Cyclist of mass M at speed v on an unbanked circular road of radius r — find the lean angle.
Weight = Mg (downward); Centrifugal force = Mv^2/r (outward)
Torques about A: N and f pass through A, so their torques = 0
Torque of weight = Mg(AD) clockwise; Torque of centrifugal force = (Mv^2/r)(CD) anticlockwise
theta = arctan(v^2 / rg) from the vertical
tan theta = v squared over r g
Contribution of one slice: dI = x squared dm
Sum over particles becomes an integral over the body
I = I-naught + M d squared
Q: Find the moment of inertia of a uniform ring of mass M and radius R about a diameter.
Iz = M R squared
Ring is uniform, so Ix = Iy
Iz = Ix + Iy = 2 Ix
I about a diameter = M R squared over 2  (disc: M R squared over 4)
Q: Solid cylinder, mass M, radius R. Find I about a parallel axis on the surface.
I = I0 + M d^2,  d = R
Q: Find the radius of gyration of a uniform disc of radius r about its axis
I = M k^2  so  k = sqrt(I / M)
k = sqrt((1/2) M r^2 / M) = sqrt(r^2 / 2)
k = r / sqrt(2)
Lightest spin axis passes through centre of mass
l = r \times p, angular momentum about O
r-perp = perpendicular distance from O to line
single particle: l = m v r

events.title: From one particle to a whole body

events.text: l-i = m-i r-i squared omega
L = (sum of m r squared) times omega = I omega
Q: Particle moves in a circle of radius r with speed v. Find its angular momentum about the axis.
Choose origin at centre of circle
r is along the radius, v is along the tangent
r is perpendicular to v
r cross p is perpendicular to both r and p, so it points along the axis
Angular momentum about the axis = m v r
Q: A rigid body rotates about axis AB with angular velocity omega. Find its total angular momentum about AB.
v-i = r-i · omega
l-i = m-i · v-i · r-i = m-i · r-i² · omega
L = sum of m-i · r-i² · omega
L = (sum of m-i · r-i²) · omega = I · omega
L = I · omega
L = I omega
External torque = 0 means L stays constant
Q: First wheel spins at angular speed omega; identical wheel at rest dropped on same axle. Find common angular speed.
L initial = I omega + 0 = I omega
Friction is internal; no external torque, so L is conserved.
I omega = 2 I omega prime
omega prime = omega / 2
I down, omega up, L fixed
Angular impulse = area under the torque-time graph
Particle KE = one half m v squared, with v = omega r
Rotational KE is just one half m v squared summed over all particles
Sum of m r squared = moment of inertia I
Power delivered: P = Gamma times omega
Motion = translation of CM + pure spin about CM
Pseudo torque about CM proportional to sum of m times r, which is zero
Torque = I alpha holds about the CM even when it accelerates
One rotation moves the wheel forward by 2 pi R
Centre moves straight, rim loops
Q: In pure rolling, find the velocity of the contact point, the centre, and the topmost point.
Pure rolling: velocity of contact point = 0
v of centre = omega times R
v of topmost point = 2 omega R = 2 times v of centre
contact = 0, centre = omega R, top = 2 omega R = 2 v of centre
Q: A wheel of radius r rolls without slipping; angular velocity omega, car velocity v, with v = omega r. Find the velocity of the contact point with respect to the road.
v(contact, road) = v(contact, car) + v(car, road)
v(contact, road) = -omega r + v
= -omega r + omega r = 0
v(contact, road) = 0
Q: When v is greater than omega r, what motion does the wheel undergo at the contact point?
velocity of contact w.r.t. road = (-omega r) + v
Q: If v is less than omega r, what happens at the point of contact?
velocity of contact with respect to road = minus omega r plus v
velocity of contact with respect to road = minus omega r plus v, which is less than zero, so this is rolling with backward slipping
speed of centre = R times spin rate
Two motions at once: spin + glide
K = spin energy about center + forward energy of whole mass
Rolling KE = spin about center + glide of center, locked by v = R-omega
position = r naught + r relative to c.m.
