chapters.narration_text:
<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_1>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_1:rotating_body_axis>> Pick up any solid thing near you — a book, a phone, a tennis racket — and pin it with two fingers at two points. Now try to move it. You'll find you simply can't slide it around. The only motion left to you is a spin — and that spin is exactly what we call rotation. <<SECTION:The axis of rotation|id=sec-1>> Those two fixed fingertips <<TRACE:axis-line>> define a straight line, and the whole body turns about that line. We give it a name — the axis of rotation. Now watch one single particle <<FOCUS:particle-far>> out near the edge of the body as it spins. <<UNFOCUS>> What kind of path do you think it carves out? <<PAUSE:long>> It travels <<TRACE:circle-far>> in a perfect circle. And here's the key: to find the centre of that circle, <<TRACE:perpendicular-far>> drop a straight perpendicular from the particle onto the axis. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Centre of each circle = foot of perpendicular to the axis|id=key-1>> The <<FOCUS:foot-far>> foot of that perpendicular, sitting right on the axis, is the centre of the particle's circular path. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Radius = distance from axis|id=text-1>> So the radius of a particle's circle is just <<FOCUS:perpendicular-far>> its distance from the axis. A particle far out <<FOCUS:particle-far+circle-far>> sweeps a big circle. A particle close to the axis <<FOCUS:particle-near+circle-near>> sweeps a tiny circle, and a particle sitting right on the axis doesn't move at all. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the puzzle. The far particle <<FOCUS:circle-far>> races around a huge circle while the <<FOCUS:circle-near>> near one barely budges. <<UNFOCUS>> Yet they're locked in the same rigid body. Who finishes their lap first? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> They finish together — exactly together. Because the body is rigid, every particle sweeps the same angle in the same time. The far one just goes faster to keep up. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Each particle: centre on axis, same time per turn|id=text-2>> Think of a swinging door: the hinge line is the axis, the edge sweeps a wide arc, points near the hinge barely move, and the whole door turns as one. <<WRITE_KEY:Same angle, same time — that's why we measure rotation by angle|id=key-2>> So rotation is this: every particle on its own circle, every centre on the axis, and every single one sweeping equal angles in equal times. That last fact is why we'll soon describe spinning bodies not by distance, but by angle. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_2>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_2:spinning_disc_angle>> Look at a ceiling fan. The tip of the blade is racing, the middle is dawdling, the center barely moves at all. Yet somehow we say the fan spins at one single speed. How can one number describe all of that? <<PAUSE:long>> Here is the trick. Instead of asking how far each point travels, let's ask how much it turns. Take a particle <<FOCUS:particle-inner>> near the center and a particle <<FOCUS:particle-outer>> out at the rim. <<FOCUS:radius-inner-start+radius-outer-start>> Draw a line from the axis out to each particle at the start. <<UNFOCUS>> This line is our pointer, recording where each particle begins. <<SECTION:Angular position|id=sec-1>> Now let the disc spin for a moment. Each pointer swings around to a new position, <<FOCUS:radius-inner-now+radius-outer-now>> sweeping out an angle as it goes. That swept angle is what we call the <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> angular position, theta. <<UNFOCUS>> And here is the beautiful part. Watch <<FOCUS:radius-inner-now>> the inner particle's angle and <<FOCUS:radius-outer-now>> the outer particle's angle. <<WRITE_KEY:Every particle sweeps the same angle theta|id=key-1>> They are <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> exactly the same. <<UNFOCUS>> The rim point travelled much farther, but it turned through the very same angle. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> Because that angle is <<FOCUS:angle-theta>> shared by every single particle in the body, one number describes the whole spin. That one number, theta, is the angular position of <<FOCUS:disc-body>> the entire rigid body. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:theta measured in radians, full turn = two pi|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> We measure theta in radians. If a particle goes all the way around once, every particle does too, and the body has turned through two pi radians, one full revolution. One full trip around the circle means the body has turned through two pi radians. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\theta = 2\pi \text{ (one revolution)}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<SECTION:Angular velocity|id=sec-2>> So that is where the body is. But how fast is it spinning? Let the body turn a little extra, a small change in angle, delta theta, during a small slice of time, delta t. The average angular velocity is simply that change in angle divided by the time it took. In words: how much it turned, shared over how long. <<PAUSE:short>> Average angular velocity is the change in angle divided by the time taken. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\omega_{avg} = \dfrac{\Delta\theta}{\Delta t}|id=eq-2|boxed>> But a fan can speed up partway through. If I want the speed at one exact instant, what do I do? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's an example from the chapter. The motor of an engine is rotating about its axis with an angular velocity of one hundred revolutions per minute, which is ten pi over three radians per second. After being switched off, it comes to rest in fifteen seconds. Assuming constant angular deceleration, we want the number of revolutions it makes before coming to rest. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Motor at 100 rev/min comes to rest in 15 s under constant deceleration. Find revolutions made.|id=ex-q-1>> Shrink the time interval to an instant and the average becomes the instantaneous angular velocity, the derivative of theta with respect to time. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\omega = \dfrac{d\theta}{dt}|id=eq-3|boxed>> Let's list what we know. The initial angular velocity is ten pi over three radians per second, the final angular velocity is zero, and the time interval is fifteen seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:omega_0 = 10pi/3 rad/s, omega = 0, t = 15 s|id=ex-step-1-1>> First we find the angular acceleration. Using the equation omega equals omega naught plus alpha times t, we set zero equal to ten pi over three plus alpha times fifteen. Solving, the angular acceleration comes out to minus two pi over nine radians per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:0 = 10pi/3 + alpha(15)  =>  alpha = -2pi/9 rad/s^2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now we find the angle rotated using theta equals omega naught times t plus one half alpha t squared. That's ten pi over three times fifteen, minus one half times two pi over nine times fifteen squared. <<WRITE_STEP:theta = omega_0 t + (1/2) alpha t^2 = (10pi/3)(15) - (1/2)(2pi/9)(15)^2|id=ex-step-1-3>> Working that out gives twenty-five pi radians, which is twelve point five revolutions. So the answer is twelve point five revolutions. Hence the motor rotates through twelve point five revolutions before coming to rest. <<WRITE_ANSWER:theta = 25pi rad = 12.5 revolutions|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Starting from rest, a fan takes five seconds to attain its maximum speed of four hundred revolutions per minute. Assuming constant angular acceleration, we want to find the time taken to attain half the maximum speed, which is two hundred revolutions per minute. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Fan from rest reaches 400 rpm in 5 s (constant angular acceleration). Find time to reach 200 rpm.|id=ex-q-1>> Let the angular acceleration be alpha. Since the fan starts from rest, its initial speed is zero, so applying the relation final speed equals initial speed plus alpha times time, we get four hundred revolutions per minute equals zero plus alpha times five seconds. <<WRITE_STEP:400 rev/min = 0 + alpha x 5 s   ... (i)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now let t be the time taken to reach two hundred revolutions per minute, which is half the maximum. Again starting from rest, we write two hundred revolutions per minute equals zero plus alpha times t. <<WRITE_STEP:200 rev/min = 0 + alpha x t   ... (ii)|id=ex-step-1-2>> Dividing equation one by equation two, the alpha cancels out, and four hundred over two hundred gives two, equal to five seconds over t. So two equals five seconds over t. <<WRITE_STEP:2 = (5 s) / t|id=ex-step-1-3>> Solving for t, we find t equals five seconds divided by two, which is two point five seconds. And so the fan reaches half its maximum speed in two point five seconds. <<WRITE_ANSWER:t = 2.5 seconds|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A bucket is being lowered into a well by a rope passing over a fixed pulley of radius ten centimeters. The rope does not slip on the pulley. At one instant the bucket is going down at a speed of twenty centimeters per second and has an acceleration of four point zero meters per second squared. We want the angular velocity and angular acceleration of the pulley. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Pulley radius 10 cm, rope does not slip. Bucket speed 20 cm/s, acceleration 4.0 m/s2. Find pulley's omega and alpha.|id=ex-q-1>> Because the rope does not slip, the rim of the pulley moves exactly with the bucket, so the linear speed v of the rim equals the bucket's speed of twenty centimeters per second. We get the angular velocity from omega equals v over r. That's twenty centimeters per second divided by ten centimeters, which gives two radians per second. <<WRITE_STEP:omega = v / r = (20 cm/s) / (10 cm) = 2 rad/s|id=ex-step-1-1>> The same no-slip condition links the accelerations, so the angular acceleration is alpha equals a over r. That's four point zero meters per second squared divided by ten centimeters, which gives forty radians per second squared. So the pulley spins at two radians per second and speeds up at forty radians per second squared. <<WRITE_STEP:alpha = a / r = (4.0 m/s2) / (10 cm) = 40 rad/s2|id=ex-step-1-2>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:omega = 2 rad/s, alpha = 40 rad/s2|id=ex-ans-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> I shrink the time slice down until it is vanishingly small. In that limit, delta theta over delta t becomes the derivative, d theta by d t, the instantaneous angular velocity, omega. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:omega = d theta / d t, one number for the whole body|id=key-2>> And just like theta, this omega belongs to the entire body at once. The fan tip and the fan center share one angular velocity, even though their actual speeds differ wildly. That is the whole power of describing rotation by angle.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_3>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_3:fan_spinning>> Flip on a ceiling fan and <<FOCUS:fan-blade-top+fan-blade-bottom>> the blades whirl faster and faster, yet <<FOCUS:fan-center>> the center never moves. <<UNFOCUS>> That is a genuine puzzle. <<PAUSE:long>> Watch the hub. It is <<FOCUS:fan-center>> bolted to the ceiling, so it stays perfectly still while the blades pick up speed around it. <<WRITE_TEXT:spin speeding up = angular acceleration|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> This speeding up of the spin has a name. We call it <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> angular acceleration. <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the key observation. If <<FOCUS:fan-center>> the center of the fan stays at rest, then the outside forces on the fan must all add up to exactly zero. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Angular acceleration possible even with zero net force|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So we have discovered something surprising: you can have angular acceleration even when the total external force is zero. <<PAUSE:short>> Look at how that works. <<FOCUS:force-up>> Push the top blade one way, and an equal push sends <<FOCUS:force-down>> the bottom blade the opposite way. <<FOCUS:force-up+force-down>> The two forces cancel. Their sum is zero, so the center never budges, but both pushes still <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> drive the blades around the same way. <<UNFOCUS>> But now flip the question around. If zero net force can spin a fan, why must you bother switching it on at all? <<PAUSE:long>> Why does a wheel on the floor not just start spinning the instant you wish it would? Why must your muscles do work? <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:No angular acceleration without an external force|id=key-2>> Here is the resolution: you cannot get angular acceleration without an external force. The fan needs that push. <<PAUSE:short>> So both things are true at once. Net force can be zero, yet force must still be present. What really matters is not where the forces point, but how they twist. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:torque = the twisting effect of a force|id=text-2>> That twisting effect is the real cause of angular acceleration, and it has a name we meet next: torque. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_4>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_4:door_torque_topview>> Push a door <<FOCUS:hinge-axis>> right next to its hinge, as hard as you like, and it barely moves. Push <<FOCUS:point-P>> at the far edge with one finger, and it swings open. <<UNFOCUS>> Same door, same muscles — so why does where you push change everything? <<SECTION:Turning effect of a force|id=sec-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The secret is <<FOCUS:position-vector-r>> the distance from the hinge. Here is the arrow from the hinge to the spot where you push — call it r. Now here is your push, <<FOCUS:force-vector-f>> the force F, pointing straight off the face of the door. The turning effect — physicists call it torque — grows <<FOCUS:position-vector-r>> when r is longer and when your push is <<FOCUS:force-vector-f>> more perpendicular to the door. <<WRITE_TEXT:torque = turning effect of a force|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> Watch what happens if you push <<FOCUS:force-along-door>> straight along the door, toward the hinge instead — this faded arrow. The door <<FOCUS:torque-arrow>> doesn't turn at all, even though you're pushing hard. <<UNFOCUS>> So direction matters as much as distance, and there's one clean operation that captures both at once. Torque equals <<FOCUS:position-vector-r+force-vector-f>> the position vector r crossed with the force F, a vector pointing along the axis of the spin. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{\Gamma} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Torque is r crossed with F|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> We write the torque as r crossed with F — the cross product. It points <<FOCUS:torque-arrow>> along the axis the door turns about, and its length measures the turning strength. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The cross product hides a beautiful shortcut. Drop a perpendicular from the hinge onto the line of your push — <<TRACE:perp-distance>> this dashed distance. <<UNFOCUS>> The size of the torque is r times F times the sine of the angle between them, which is just the force times the perpendicular distance to the axis. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = r F \sin\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = F \times d_{\perp}|id=eq-1>> The torque is simply your force times that perpendicular distance — push farther out, or more squarely, and <<FOCUS:perp-distance>> the perpendicular distance grows. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now a subtle question: to measure torque you needed an origin on the axis. Would picking a different point on the hinge line give a different answer? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It does not. <<FOCUS:hinge-axis>> Slide your origin anywhere up or down the axis and the extra piece you add points along the axis, contributing nothing to the spin — so the torque about the line stays exactly the same. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So torque is r crossed with F: push far from the axis and push perpendicular for the strongest turn — and you're free to choose any convenient origin on the axis.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_6>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_6:ladder_equilibrium>> A ladder leans against a wall, perfectly still, and the forces on it add up to zero — so why does a ladder ever slide out from under you? <<PAUSE:long>> Let's lay out every push and pull on this ladder. Gravity pulls its <<FOCUS:weight-force>> weight straight down at the middle. <<FOCUS:ground-normal>> The ground pushes up at the foot, and <<FOCUS:wall-normal>> the wall pushes back horizontally at the top, while <<FOCUS:friction-force>> friction at the foot grips toward the wall. <<SECTION:Two conditions for equilibrium|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the first rule. If the total force is zero, then by F equals m a the acceleration is zero, so the ladder's center doesn't speed up in any direction. <<PAUSE:short>> But watch — I can balance all the forces and still let the ladder spin. Could a body have zero net force and yet start to rotate? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Yes it can. Forces that cancel as arrows can still twist a body — think of two hands spinning a steering wheel: zero net force, plenty of turning. So we need a second rule: zero total torque. Since torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration, zero torque means zero spin-up. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Equilibrium needs BOTH: zero net force AND zero net torque|id=key-1>> So to truly sit still a body needs both: zero total force in every direction, and zero total torque about any line. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Forces in one plane|id=sec-2>> Notice <<FOCUS:weight-force+ground-normal+wall-normal+friction-force>> all four forces here lie flat in a single plane, the plane of the page. <<WRITE_TEXT:Sum Fx = 0, Sum Fy = 0|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That collapses the force condition to just two equations: the horizontal forces cancel, and the vertical forces cancel. <<PAUSE:short>> Because all the forces lie flat in one plane, the force condition becomes just two statements: the horizontal forces cancel and the vertical forces cancel. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sum F_x = 0, \quad \sum F_y = 0|id=eq-1|boxed>> And the torque? Every force lies in the plane, so the only twisting it can do is about an axis sticking out of the page. That leaves one torque equation. The only way these in-plane forces can twist the body is about an axis poking out of the page, so rotational balance is a single equation: the total torque about that axis is zero. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sum \Gamma_z = 0|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the beautiful part. Because the body is balanced, you may take that torque about ANY point you like — <<FOCUS:foot-pivot>> pick the foot, and <<FOCUS:ground-normal+friction-force>> the ground's forces vanish from the equation, making the unknowns easy to find. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Coplanar forces: take torque about ANY point and still get zero|id=key-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> So a ladder slides only when these balances break — and the smart move is always to take torques about the cleverest point. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_7>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_7:cyclist_lean_forces>> Why do you lean your bike into a turn? Try staying bolt upright through a sharp corner, and you'll feel yourself toppling outward. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Why leaning is forced|id=sec-1>> To travel in a circle, something must constantly pull you toward the centre, otherwise you'd shoot off in a straight line. On a flat road, that inward pull can only come from one place: <<FOCUS:friction-vector>> the friction where your tyres grip the ground. <<WRITE_TEXT:Friction at the tyres supplies the inward force|id=text-1>> So <<FOCUS:friction-vector+contact-point>> friction at the contact point is your inward force. <<UNFOCUS>> Without leaning, you'd ride upright and friction would still be there, pulling your wheels inward. Here's the problem with staying upright: that <<FOCUS:friction-vector>> inward friction acts down at the road, but your body's <<FOCUS:weight-vector+centre-of-mass>> weight acts up at the centre of mass. <<UNFOCUS>> Those two together would twist you, and you'd tip over the outside. <<WRITE_KEY:Lean inward so friction can curve your path|id=key-1>> So <<FOCUS:lean-line+cyclist-body>> you lean inward. <<UNFOCUS>> To go round a flat curve, a cyclist must lean so the ground's friction can supply the inward force that bends his path into a circle. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Balancing the torques|id=sec-2>> Now let's find the exact angle. Look at <<FOCUS:contact-point>> the contact point A where the tyre meets the road. Both <<FOCUS:normal-vector+friction-vector>> the normal force and the friction act right through A, so about that point they create no twist at all. That leaves only two forces that can twist you about A: <<FOCUS:weight-vector>> your weight pulling down, and the inward force needed for the circle. <<UNFOCUS>> If your lean is correct, their twists exactly cancel, and you ride steadily. <<PAUSE:short>> So how much should you lean? Does it depend on how fast you ride, or how tight the bend is? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Weight times horizontal offset equals inward force times height|id=step-1>> Picture the <<TRACE:lean-line>> leaning line from A up to the centre of mass. The weight twists you one way, the inward force the other; setting them equal, the horizontal pull is your weight times <<FOCUS:lean-angle>> the tangent of the lean angle. <<UNFOCUS>> The weight's twist about the contact point balances the inward force's twist, so weight times the tangent of the lean angle equals the mass times v squared over r. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Mg\tan\theta = \frac{Mv^2}{r}|id=eq-1|boxed>> And the inward force a circle demands is the mass times v squared over r. Divide it by the weight, the mass cancels, and out drops a beautifully simple rule. Here's an example from the chapter. A cyclist moves at speed v on a horizontal circular road of radius r, and the road is not banked. We treat the cycle plus rider together as one system of total mass M. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Cyclist of mass M at speed v on an unbanked circular road of radius r — find the lean angle.|id=ex-q-1>> Dividing through by the weight, the mass cancels and the lean angle depends only on speed, radius, and gravity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\tan\theta = \frac{v^2}{rg}|id=eq-2|boxed>> Working in the rotating frame, the system is at rest, so the total external force and total external torque must both be zero. Two forces act through the body: <<FOCUS:weight-vector>> the weight, equal to M times g, acting downward, and <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass>> the centrifugal force, equal to M times v squared divided by r, acting outward through the center of mass. <<WRITE_STEP:Weight = Mg (downward); Centrifugal force = Mv^2/r (outward)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we take <<FOCUS:contact-point>> torques about the contact point A. The <<FOCUS:normal-vector+friction-vector>> normal force N and the friction f both pass through A, so their torques about A are zero. <<UNFOCUS>> That leaves just the weight and the centrifugal force. <<WRITE_STEP:Torques about A: N and f pass through A, so their torques = 0|id=ex-step-1-2>> The torque of the weight about A is M g times the distance A D, in the clockwise direction. The torque of the centrifugal force is M v squared over r times the distance C D, in the anticlockwise direction. <<WRITE_STEP:Torque of weight = Mg(AD) clockwise; Torque of centrifugal force = (Mv^2/r)(CD) anticlockwise|id=ex-step-1-3>> For rotational equilibrium the two torques are equal, so M g times A D equals M v squared over r times C D. Dividing, the ratio A D over C D equals v squared over r g, and that ratio is exactly the tangent of the lean angle theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Mg(AD) = \frac{Mv^2}{r}(CD) \;\Rightarrow\; \tan\theta = \frac{AD}{CD} = \frac{v^2}{rg}|id=ex-eq-1>> And so the answer is that the cyclist bends at an angle theta whose tangent equals v squared divided by r times g — that is, theta equals the inverse tangent of v squared over r g, <<FOCUS:lean-angle+vertical-ref>> measured from the vertical. <<WRITE_ANSWER:theta = arctan(v^2 / rg) from the vertical|id=ex-ans-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> The tangent of the lean angle equals v squared over r times g. Go faster, or take a tighter bend, and you must lean further in. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:tan theta = v squared over r g|id=key-2>> So the next time you carve round a corner, remember: that lean isn't a trick, it's geometry. The tangent of theta equals v squared over r times g tells you exactly how hard to lean. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_14>>
A solid rod and a ring of exactly the same mass — spin them both, and one fights back far harder than the other. Why? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Where the resistance lives|id=sec-1>> The answer is that what matters isn't just how much mass you have, but where that mass sits relative to the axis you spin around. <<PAUSE:short>> Take each tiny piece of the object, multiply its mass by the square of its distance from the axis, and add every one of those up — that total is the moment of inertia. <<PAUSE:short>> Take each tiny piece, multiply its mass by the square of its distance from the axis, and add them all up. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2|id=eq-1>> For a handful of separate masses this is easy: just compute mass times distance squared for each one and add them together. Notice that square sitting in the formula — it's why mass placed far out is so punishing. <<PAUSE:short>> Double the distance and that piece contributes four times as much resistance, even though its mass hasn't changed at all. But real objects — rods, plates, rings, spheres — aren't a few dots. They're continuous lumps of matter. So how do we add up infinitely many pieces? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_14:sliced_rod>> Here's the beautiful trick from calculus. We <<FOCUS:mass-element+mass-hatch>> slice the object into elements so tiny that every point in one slice sits at essentially the same distance from the axis. Look at <<FOCUS:mass-element>> one thin slice of this rod, <<FOCUS:distance-x>> a distance x from the axis, carrying <<FOCUS:dm-label>> a tiny mass we call dm. <<WRITE_STEP:Contribution of one slice: dI = x squared dm|id=step-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> That single slice contributes its mass dm times x squared, exactly like one particle in our sum. <<WRITE_KEY:Sum over particles becomes an integral over the body|id=key-1>> Now add up every slice as it <<FOCUS:rod-body+length-label>> slides from the axis along the whole length — the sum becomes an integral over the entire body. <<PAUSE:short>> Add up every infinitesimal slice's mass times its distance squared, and <<FOCUS:integral-form>> the sum becomes an integral over the whole body. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I = \int r^2 \, dm|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:I = \int r^2 \, dm|id=eq-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> And that's the master tool: integrate r squared dm across the object, and you can find the moment of inertia of any shape you like. So back to our puzzle: the ring keeps all its mass out at the rim, far from the centre, while the rod spreads mass right down to the axis. Same mass, but the ring's r squared is bigger everywhere — so the ring fights back harder. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_15>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_15:parallel_axes_figure>> You already worked out how hard a ring is to spin about its centre. Now I slide the axis out to the rim. Do you really have to redo the entire calculation from scratch? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:body-outline>> Here is the body, and here is <<FOCUS:axis-cm+centre-of-mass>> the line through its centre of mass, the axis you already solved. <<SECTION:Parallel Axes Theorem|id=sec-1>> Now I want a different axis, <<FOCUS:axis-parallel>> this one over here, perfectly parallel to the first, but shifted off to the side. The only thing that changed is <<FOCUS:axis-cm+axis-parallel>> this gap between the two lines. Call that <<FOCUS:distance-d>> perpendicular distance d. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And here is the beautiful part: you do not start over. You take the answer you already have and add a single correction term. <<PAUSE:short>> In words: the moment of inertia about the new line equals the moment of inertia about the centre-of-mass line, plus the whole mass times the square of the distance you moved. <<PAUSE:short>> The moment of inertia about the new line equals the moment of inertia about the centre-of-mass line plus the mass times the square of the distance between them. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I = I_0 + Md^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:I = I-naught + M d squared|id=key-1>> So I equals I-naught <<FOCUS:distance-d>> plus M d squared. <<UNFOCUS>> That extra piece is exactly the cost of moving the axis away from the centre. <<PAUSE:short>> Notice that M d squared is always positive. Mass is positive, and a squared distance can never be negative. So what does that tell you about spinning an object off-centre versus through its centre? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It is always harder. Moving the axis away from the centre of mass can only increase the moment of inertia, never decrease it. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have a uniform ring of mass M and radius R, and we want the moment of inertia about a diameter. We already know the moment of inertia about the central perpendicular axis through the centre is M times R squared. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the moment of inertia of a uniform ring of mass M and radius R about a diameter.|id=ex-q-1>> Let's set up our axes. Take two mutually perpendicular diameters of the ring as the X and Y axes, and the line perpendicular to the plane of the ring through the centre as the Z axis. The moment of inertia about the Z axis is M times R squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Iz = M R squared|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, because the ring is uniform, all of its diameters are equivalent, so the moment of inertia about the X axis equals the moment of inertia about the Y axis. That is, Ix equals Iy. <<WRITE_STEP:Ring is uniform, so Ix = Iy|id=ex-step-1-2>> Next we apply the perpendicular axes theorem, which says Iz equals Ix plus Iy. Since Ix equals Iy, this becomes Iz equals two times Ix. <<WRITE_STEP:Iz = Ix + Iy = 2 Ix|id=ex-step-1-3>> So Ix equals Iz over two, which is M times R squared divided by two. And the answer is: the moment of inertia of the ring about a diameter is M times R squared divided by two. By a similar argument, the moment of inertia of a uniform disc about a diameter is M times R squared divided by four. <<WRITE_ANSWER:I about a diameter = M R squared over 2  (disc: M R squared over 4)|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. We have a solid cylinder of mass M and radius R, and we want its moment of inertia about a line parallel to the axis of the cylinder and lying on the surface of the cylinder. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Solid cylinder, mass M, radius R. Find I about a parallel axis on the surface.|id=ex-q-1>> We start with what we know. The moment of inertia of the cylinder about its own axis is M times R squared divided by two. <<WRITE_STEP:I0 = M R^2 / 2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we use the parallel axes theorem, which says I equals I-naught plus M times d squared. Since the new axis is parallel and sits on the surface, the shift distance d equals R. <<WRITE_STEP:I = I0 + M d^2,  d = R|id=ex-step-1-2>> Substituting, we get M R squared over two plus M times R squared, which adds up to three halves times M times R squared. <<WRITE_STEP:I = M R^2 / 2 + M R^2 = (3/2) M R^2|id=ex-step-1-3>> The same trick works for a solid sphere. Its moment of inertia about its centre is two fifths M times R squared, so about a tangent it becomes two fifths M R squared plus M R squared, which is seven fifths times M times R squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Sphere: (2/5) M R^2 + M R^2 = (7/5) M R^2|id=ex-step-1-4>> And the answer for the cylinder is three halves times M times R squared. <<WRITE_ANSWER:I = (3/2) M R^2|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Take a uniform disc of radius r, and let's find its radius of gyration about its own axis. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the radius of gyration of a uniform disc of radius r about its axis|id=ex-q-1>> The radius of gyration k is defined by the relation I equals M times k squared, so k is the square root of I over M. For a uniform disc about its axis, the moment of inertia I equals one half M r squared. <<WRITE_STEP:I = M k^2  so  k = sqrt(I / M)|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:I = (1/2) M r^2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Substituting, k equals the square root of one half M r squared divided by M, which is the square root of r squared over two. So the radius of gyration of a uniform disc of radius r about its axis is r divided by the square root of two. <<WRITE_STEP:k = sqrt((1/2) M r^2 / M) = sqrt(r^2 / 2)|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_ANSWER:k = r / sqrt(2)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Lightest spin axis passes through centre of mass|id=text-1>> The centre of mass is the single easiest place to put the axis. Every parallel line away from it costs you M d squared more. There is a companion shortcut for thin flat plates, the perpendicular axes theorem, that adds the moments about two in-plane axes to get the one sticking straight out, but the parallel axes idea is the workhorse you will reach for again and again.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_8>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_8:particle_about_o>> A ball flying in a perfectly straight line, never curving — and yet, from where you're standing, it can carry spin. Let's see how that's even possible. <<FOCUS:particle-P>> Here's our particle P, just cruising along <<FOCUS:motion-line>> this straight line <<FOCUS:momentum-vector-p>> with some momentum p, which is simply its mass times its velocity. Now <<FOCUS:point-O>> I pick a point O to watch from, sitting off to the side. <<UNFOCUS>> The whole story depends on this choice, and that's the part people miss. <<PAUSE:short>> I draw an arrow from O straight to the particle. <<FOCUS:position-vector-r>> That's the position vector r — it tells me where the particle is relative to my chosen point. <<UNFOCUS>> So why would a straight mover have any spin about O at all? Watch what happens to that arrow r as the particle slides along. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:l = r \times p, angular momentum about O|id=key-1>> <<TRACE:position-vector-r>> The arrow r swings around as the particle moves, even though the particle goes straight. <<UNFOCUS>> That swinging is the spin. We capture it as the cross product r cross p, and we call it angular momentum l. <<PAUSE:short>> The angular momentum of the particle about O is the cross product of the position vector r and the momentum p. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{l} = \vec{r} \times \vec{p}|id=eq-1|boxed>> Because it's a cross product of two vectors, l is itself a vector, pointing <<FOCUS:position-vector-r+momentum-vector-p>> perpendicular to both r and p — out of the page in this case. <<SECTION:How big is it?|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now let's get its size. <<FOCUS:theta-angle>> The angle between r and p is theta, and the cross product brings in the sine of that angle. <<WRITE_TEXT:r-perp = perpendicular distance from O to line|id=text-1>> Here's the beautiful simplification: r times sine theta is just <<FOCUS:perp-distance>> the perpendicular distance from O down to the line of motion. <<UNFOCUS>> Call it r-perpendicular. <<PAUSE:short>> So the size of the angular momentum is simply the momentum m v multiplied by that <<FOCUS:perp-distance>> perpendicular distance r-perpendicular. <<UNFOCUS>> No angles to fuss over. <<PAUSE:short>> The magnitude of the angular momentum equals the momentum, mass times velocity, times the perpendicular distance from O to the line of motion. <<WRITE_EQUATION:l = m v\, r_{\perp}|id=eq-2|boxed>> And notice — if I'd <<FOCUS:point-O+motion-line>> chosen O sitting right on the line, the perpendicular distance would be zero, and the spin would vanish. <<UNFOCUS>> That's why angular momentum always belongs to a chosen point. So a straight-flying particle has angular momentum about a point off its path, equal to its momentum times the perpendicular reach of that path. That single idea is the seed of all of rotational mechanics.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_9>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_9:particle_in_circle>> A single spinning ball and an entire spinning wheel — could one neat equation describe the angular momentum of both? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:One particle in a circle|id=sec-1>> Let's start small. Here is a single ball whisking around <<FOCUS:circle-path+radius-vector>> a circular path of radius r, and right now it is <<FOCUS:velocity-vector>> moving with speed v. <<UNFOCUS>> We want its angular momentum about the axis through the centre. Here's the clever trick: we are free to put the origin anywhere on that axis, so we plant it <<FOCUS:axis-center>> right at the centre of the circle. <<UNFOCUS>> Now look what happens. The position vector r <<FOCUS:radius-vector>> points straight outward along a radius, while the <<FOCUS:velocity-vector>> velocity points along the tangent — the way the ball is actually heading. And those two directions are <<FOCUS:right-angle-mark>> perfectly perpendicular to each other. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Because angular momentum is r crossed with the momentum p, and these are at right angles, the magnitude is simply m times v times r. <<WRITE_KEY:single particle: l = m v r|id=key-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> For a single particle, since the radius and velocity are perpendicular, its angular momentum is just its mass times its speed times its radius. <<WRITE_EQUATION:l = mvr|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_9:rigid_body_axis>> <<SECTION:From one particle to a whole body|id=sec-2>> Now swap the lone ball for a real rigid body spinning about <<FOCUS:rotation-axis>> an axis we'll call AB, all of it turning together with <<FOCUS:omega-arc>> one angular velocity omega. <<UNFOCUS>> Think of the body as countless tiny particles. Pick one, <<FOCUS:particle-i>> the ith particle, going in its own <<FOCUS:orbit-i+radius-i>> circle of radius r-i around the axis. <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the key link: each particle's speed depends on how far out it sits. The further from the axis, the faster it sweeps, so its speed <<FOCUS:velocity-i>> v-i equals r-i times omega. <<UNFOCUS>> So if one particle has angular momentum m v r, then for this particle it becomes m-i times r-i omega times r-i — that is m-i r-i squared, all times omega. <<WRITE_STEP:l-i = m-i r-i squared omega|id=step-1>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Add up every particle, and omega is shared by all of them, so it factors out. What's left inside is the sum of m times r squared — and that is exactly the moment of inertia, I. <<WRITE_STEP:L = (sum of m r squared) times omega = I omega|id=step-2>> Adding up every particle and pulling out the shared angular velocity leaves the sum of mass times radius squared, which is the moment of inertia, so the total angular momentum is moment of inertia times angular velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:L = \sum m_i r_i^2 \, \omega = I\omega|id=eq-2|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose a particle is going in a circle of radius r, and at some instant the speed of the particle is v. The question is: what is the angular momentum of this particle about the axis of the circle? <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Particle moves in a circle of radius r with speed v. Find its angular momentum about the axis.|id=ex-q-1>> Since the origin can be chosen anywhere on the axis, we choose it at the centre of the circle. With that choice, the position vector r points along a radius, and the velocity v points along the tangent. <<WRITE_STEP:Choose origin at centre of circle|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:r is along the radius, v is along the tangent|id=ex-step-1-2>> Now here is the key geometric fact: a radius is always perpendicular to the tangent, so the position is perpendicular to the velocity. The angular momentum has magnitude l equals the magnitude of r cross p, which equals mass times velocity times radius, that is m v r. <<WRITE_STEP:r is perpendicular to v|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:l = |\vec{r} \times \vec{p}| = mvr|id=ex-eq-1>> Finally, r cross p is perpendicular to both r and p, and so the cross product points along the axis. That means the whole of m v r lies along the axis. <<WRITE_STEP:r cross p is perpendicular to both r and p, so it points along the axis|id=ex-step-1-4>> And so the answer is that the component of angular momentum along the axis is m v r itself. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Angular momentum about the axis = m v r|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Consider a rigid body rotating about <<FOCUS:rotation-axis>> an axis A B, and let the <<FOCUS:omega-arc>> angular velocity of the body be omega. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A rigid body rotates about axis AB with angular velocity omega. Find its total angular momentum about AB.|id=ex-q-1>> Now look at <<FOCUS:particle-i>> the i-th particle. It goes in a <<FOCUS:orbit-i+radius-i>> circle of radius r-i, with its plane perpendicular to A B. At this instant its <<FOCUS:velocity-i>> linear velocity is r-i times omega. <<WRITE_STEP:v-i = r-i · omega|id=ex-step-1-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> The angular momentum of this one particle about A B is its mass times its velocity times its radius, that is mass times r-i times omega times r-i, which equals mass times radius squared times omega. <<WRITE_STEP:l-i = m-i · v-i · r-i = m-i · r-i² · omega|id=ex-step-1-2>> The angular momentum of the whole body about A B is the sum of these contributions over all the particles. <<WRITE_STEP:L = sum of m-i · r-i² · omega|id=ex-step-1-3>> Since omega is common to every particle, we pull it out. And the sum of mass times radius squared is exactly the moment of inertia I of the body about A B. <<WRITE_STEP:L = (sum of m-i · r-i²) · omega = I · omega|id=ex-step-1-4>> And so the answer is: L equals I times omega. <<WRITE_ANSWER:L = I · omega|id=ex-ans-1>> And there it is, beautifully simple: the angular momentum of the whole body equals its moment of inertia times its angular velocity. L equals I omega. <<WRITE_KEY:L = I omega|id=key-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> Notice the lovely echo: m v r for one particle becomes I omega for the body, with I playing the role of mass and omega playing the role of speed. The same idea, scaled up to anything that spins. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_10>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_10:skater_spin>> A spinning skater <<FOCUS:arms-in>> pulls her arms in and suddenly whirls faster, and nobody pushed her. <<UNFOCUS>> So where did that extra spin come from? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:What carries the spin|id=sec-1>> To answer that, we need one quantity that measures how much rotation a system carries. We call it angular momentum, and for a body spinning about a fixed axis it is the <<FOCUS:conservation>> moment of inertia I times the angular velocity omega. <<UNFOCUS>> Angular momentum equals the moment of inertia times the angular velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{L} = I\vec{\omega}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_10:internal_torque_pair>> Here is the deep question. If I track the total angular momentum of a whole system and ask what makes it change, what does the answer depend on? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Internal torques cancel|id=sec-2>> Inside any body the particles tug on each other. Take <<FOCUS:particle-a+particle-b>> two particles, A and B. <<FOCUS:force-a-on-b>> A pushes on B, and <<FOCUS:force-b-on-a>> B pushes back on A, equally and oppositely, along <<FOCUS:join-line>> the very line that joins them. Because those two forces <<FOCUS:force-a-on-b+force-b-on-a>> lie along the same line and are equal and opposite, the twist one tries to add about the axis is exactly undone by the other. <<UNFOCUS>> Their torques cancel. <<PAUSE:short>> Now sum over every single pair in the body. The internal torques add up to zero, every push matched by its partner. Only the <<FOCUS:body-outline>> external torque survives. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the rate of change of angular momentum equals only the total external torque. That is the payoff to our question: internal forces, however violent, can never change the spin of the whole system. The rate of change of angular momentum equals only the total external torque on the system. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \vec{\Gamma}_{\text{ext}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:External torque = 0 means L stays constant|id=key-1>> And here is the beautiful consequence. If the total external torque is zero, then the rate of change is zero, which means the angular momentum simply stays constant. <<PAUSE:short>> If the total external torque is zero, the angular momentum stays constant. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{\Gamma}_{\text{ext}} = 0 \implies \vec{L} = \text{constant}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<SECTION:Back to the skater|id=sec-3>> Now return to our skater. With her arms flung wide, her mass sits far from the axis, so her moment of inertia I is large and she spins gently. The ice is nearly frictionless, so there is almost no external torque on her. That means her angular momentum, I times omega, must stay locked at the same value. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. A first wheel is rotating at an angular speed omega about its axle, which is kept vertical. Each wheel has the same moment of inertia I about that axis. A second identical wheel, initially at rest, is gently dropped onto the same axle, and the two begin rotating together. We want the common angular speed. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: First wheel spins at angular speed omega; identical wheel at rest dropped on same axle. Find common angular speed.|id=ex-q-1>> Since I times omega is fixed, when the moment of inertia shrinks the angular velocity must grow in exactly the same proportion. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2|id=eq-4|boxed>> We start by taking both wheels together as one system and writing down the total angular momentum before they couple. The first wheel contributes I times omega, and the second, being at rest, contributes zero. So the initial total angular momentum equals I times omega plus zero, which is I times omega. <<WRITE_STEP:L initial = I omega + 0 = I omega|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, when the second wheel is dropped on, the two wheels slip and rub against each other, exerting forces of friction. That friction is an internal force of the system. No external torque acts on the two-wheel system, so the total angular momentum stays unchanged. <<WRITE_STEP:Friction is internal; no external torque, so L is conserved.|id=ex-step-1-2>> After coupling, the two wheels share a common angular speed, call it omega prime, and their combined moment of inertia is two times I. So the final angular momentum is two I times omega prime. Setting initial equal to final gives I omega equals two I omega prime. <<WRITE_STEP:I omega = 2 I omega prime|id=ex-step-1-3>> Cancelling I from both sides, we solve for omega prime. And the answer is that the common angular speed is omega over two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:omega prime = omega / 2|id=ex-ans-1>> Watch what happens when she pulls her arms in. Her mass moves close to the axis, so I shrinks. To keep the product I times omega fixed, omega must shoot up. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:I down, omega up, L fixed|id=text-1>> That is the whole secret. She spins faster because her own muscles only made an internal pull, and internal forces can never touch the angular momentum.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_11>>
Give a merry-go-round one hard shove and it spins. Give it a long, gentle push and it ends up spinning just as fast. So a big twist for a short time can match a small twist for a long time. That hints that what really matters is the twist combined with how long it lasts. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_11:torque_time_graph>> <<SECTION:Angular Impulse|id=sec-1>> The twisting effort is called torque, and let us put it on a graph against time to see this clearly. Here <<FOCUS:time-axis>> time runs along the bottom, and <<FOCUS:torque-axis>> torque rises up the side. In real life the torque need not stay steady, so let us <<TRACE:torque-curve>> draw it strong at first and fading later. Now look at <<FOCUS:thin-strip>> one tiny sliver of time, so thin we can treat the torque as constant across it. The little contribution to the spin is just torque times that tiny duration. <<UNFOCUS>> How do we account for the whole push, when the torque keeps changing the entire time? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> We simply add up every thin strip across the interval. Stack them all together and they <<FOCUS:area-under-curve>> fill the whole region under the curve. <<WRITE_KEY:Angular impulse = area under the torque-time graph|id=key-1>> That shaded area is the angular impulse. <<UNFOCUS>> It is torque added up over time, and that sum is what governs the spin. <<PAUSE:short>> The angular impulse is the torque added up over every instant of the time interval, which is the area under the torque-time graph. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \Gamma \, dt|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \Gamma \, dt|id=eq-1>> In symbols, the angular impulse J is <<FOCUS:impulse-label>> the integral of the torque Gamma over the time interval. <<SECTION:The Payoff|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now here is the beautiful part. Torque is the rate at which angular momentum changes, so torque times a tiny time equals a tiny change in angular momentum. Since torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, adding up torque over time gives the total change in angular momentum, the final value minus the initial value. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = L_2 - L_1|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = L_2 - L_1|id=eq-2>> Add up all those tiny changes, and the total angular impulse is exactly the final angular momentum minus the initial one. So the change in a body's spin is never about torque alone, but always torque multiplied by how long it acts, and that equals the change in angular momentum. <<PAUSE:short>> That is why the hard shove and the long gentle push give the same final spin. They sweep out the same area, the same angular impulse, the same change in angular momentum. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_12>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_12:spinning_disc_particles>> A spinning wheel isn't going anywhere — <<FOCUS:disc-center>> its center sits perfectly still. <<UNFOCUS>> So where on earth is its energy hiding? <<PAUSE:long>> Here's the trick: a solid body is really just a huge crowd of tiny particles, all glued together, <<FOCUS:disc-body+rotation-axis>> all spinning around the same axis. Pick out just one of them — <<FOCUS:particle-i>> this little particle here, sitting <<FOCUS:radius-i>> a distance r sub i from the axis. As the body turns, this particle isn't standing still at all — it <<TRACE:circle-path-i>> races around its own little circle. <<UNFOCUS>> And we already know its speed. For circular motion, <<FOCUS:velocity-i>> the linear speed is simply <<FOCUS:omega-arc>> the angular speed omega <<FOCUS:radius-i>> times the radius, so v sub i equals omega times r sub i. <<UNFOCUS>> The linear speed of any particle equals the angular speed times its distance from the axis. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v_i = \omega r_i|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_STEP:Particle KE = one half m v squared, with v = omega r|id=step-1>> So this one particle carries kinetic energy one half <<FOCUS:particle-label>> times its mass times its speed squared — and since the speed is omega times r sub i, that becomes one half m sub i times omega squared times r sub i squared. <<UNFOCUS>> So one particle's kinetic energy is one half its mass times omega squared times its radius squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:KE_i = \tfrac{1}{2} m_i \omega^2 r_i^2|id=eq-2|boxed>> Now if one particle is this easy, what about the whole body — could we just add up the kinetic energy of every single particle inside it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Rotational KE is just one half m v squared summed over all particles|id=key-1>> That's exactly what we do. And here is the beautiful part: every particle <<FOCUS:omega-arc>> shares the very same omega, so the one half and the omega squared are common to all of them and slide right out of the sum. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> What's left trapped inside the sum is the mass of each particle multiplied by its radius squared, added across the entire body. <<WRITE_TEXT:Sum of m r squared = moment of inertia I|id=text-1>> But that sum has a name we already met — it's the moment of inertia, the letter I. It measures how the mass is spread out from the axis. <<PAUSE:short>> So the entire spinning body's energy collapses into one clean expression: one half I omega squared. <<PAUSE:short>> Adding up every particle and pulling out the common one half and omega squared leaves one half I omega squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:KE = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\sum m_i r_i^2\right)\omega^2 = \tfrac{1}{2} I \omega^2|id=eq-3|boxed>> And notice what we did and didn't do. We never invented a new kind of energy — this is still just one half m v squared, added up over every particle, with I and omega doing the bookkeeping for the whole crowd at once. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_13>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_13:spinning_wheel_torque>> When you spin a bike wheel by pushing the pedal harder and harder, you're pouring energy into it every single second — and there's a beautifully simple way to count exactly how fast. Here's our wheel, <<FOCUS:axis+wheel-body>> free to turn about this fixed axis, and <<FOCUS:torque-arrow>> a torque is acting on it, twisting it <<FOCUS:omega-arrow>> the same way it's already spinning. <<UNFOCUS>> Because that torque produces angular acceleration, the wheel spins faster and faster, and as it speeds up its rotational kinetic energy keeps climbing. Now think back to straight-line motion: when a force makes something speed up, the rate at which its kinetic energy grows is exactly the power being delivered to it. So here's the honest question — if energy is flowing into this wheel every second, how fast is it actually arriving? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Power from a torque|id=sec-1>> The rate of increase of kinetic energy IS the power, so let's just differentiate the rotational kinetic energy and see what falls out. The rotational kinetic energy is one half I omega squared, and when we ask how fast that changes, the moment of inertia I stays constant and only omega is changing. Differentiating gives I times omega times the rate of change of omega — and that rate of change of omega is just the angular acceleration alpha. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Power delivered: P = Gamma times omega|id=key-1>> But I times alpha is simply the torque Gamma, so the power is <<FOCUS:torque-arrow+omega-arrow>> torque times angular velocity, P equals Gamma times omega — that's our answer. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The power is the rate of change of one half I omega squared, which works out to I times omega times alpha, and since I times alpha is the torque, it equals torque times angular velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P = \frac{dK}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\right) = I\omega\alpha = \Gamma\omega|id=eq-1|boxed>> Look how clean that is: the power delivered by a torque is just the torque multiplied by the angular velocity, the perfect mirror of force times velocity in straight-line motion. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Work done by a torque|id=sec-2>> Now, power is work done per second, so in a tiny slice of time the little bit of work is power times that time, which is Gamma times omega times d t. But omega times d t is just <<FOCUS:dtheta-arc>> the small angle the wheel turns through, d theta — so each small bit of work is simply torque times the angle turned. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> In a tiny turn, the work done is the torque times the small angle the body rotates through. <<WRITE_EQUATION:dW = \Gamma\, d\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:W = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Gamma\, d\theta|id=eq-work>> Add up all those slices <<FOCUS:rim-point+dtheta-arc>> as the wheel turns from one angle to another, and the total work is the integral of torque with respect to angle. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So remember the pair: power is torque times angular velocity, and work is torque summed over the angle turned — the rotational twins of force times velocity and force times distance. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_16>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_16:rolling_wheel_split>> Watch <<FOCUS:rim-point>> a single dot painted on the rim of a rolling wheel. It traces <<TRACE:cycloid-path>> this strange squashed arch, speeding up, slowing down, looping over and over. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So how on earth do you do physics on a path like that? The trick is one of the most beautiful ideas in mechanics: don't fight the mess, split it. <<SECTION:Splitting the motion|id=sec-1>> First, <<FOCUS:center-mass>> follow only the center of the wheel. <<UNFOCUS>> Forget the spin for a moment. The center just <<FOCUS:center-velocity>> glides forward in a clean straight line at a steady speed. <<UNFOCUS>> That part is pure translation, the easiest motion there is. <<PAUSE:short>> Now imagine riding along with the center, sitting in a frame that moves with it. From that seat, the center looks still, and the <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> wheel is simply spinning in place. <<WRITE_KEY:Motion = translation of CM + pure spin about CM|id=key-1>> So the whole messy motion is just two simple things added together: <<FOCUS:center-velocity>> the center translating, <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> plus pure rotation about that center. <<PAUSE:short>> Put them back together and <<FOCUS:rim-point+cycloid-path>> the rim point's looping path reappears, but now we understand it: glide plus spin. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> But here's the catch that worries a careful physicist. The frame riding with the center is accelerating, and our rotation law was proved only for inertial frames. <<PAUSE:long>> In an accelerating frame, every particle feels a pseudo force, and those usually create a pseudo torque that would wreck our equation. So does torque equals I times alpha still survive? <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Pseudo torque about CM proportional to sum of m times r, which is zero|id=step-1>> Here is the gift. Add up the pseudo torques about the center of mass, and they depend on the sum of mass times position measured from the center, which is exactly zero by definition of the center of mass. <<PAUSE:short>> The sum of each particle's mass times its position measured from the center of mass is always zero, which is exactly why the pseudo torque vanishes. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sum m_i \vec{r}_i = 0|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:Torque = I alpha holds about the CM even when it accelerates|id=key-2>> So the pseudo torque cancels perfectly. Torque equals I times alpha holds about the center of mass even while that center is accelerating. External torque about the center of mass equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration, and this still holds even in the accelerating center of mass frame. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma_{ext} = I\alpha|id=eq-2|boxed>> That is why <<FOCUS:center-mass>> the center of mass is the magic axis. <<UNFOCUS>> Treat the center with Newton's law for translation, treat the spin with torque equals I times alpha, and add them. Any rolling, tumbling, flying body bends to this one trick.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_17>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_17:rolling_wheel_cycloid>> <<FOCUS:marked-spoke>> Paint one spoke of your bicycle wheel black, and right now it points straight down at the road. <<UNFOCUS>> After one full pedal, that black spoke is pointing straight down again, in exactly the same way. So how far down the road did you travel? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the surprising answer: you moved forward by exactly <<TRACE:rim-path>> the distance around the rim. <<UNFOCUS>> That is the circumference, two times pi times the radius of the wheel. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Rolling|id=sec-1>> Think of it like this: the wheel never slips, so it <<FOCUS:wheel-circle+road-line>> lays the rim down onto the road like unrolling a piece of tape. <<UNFOCUS>> One full turn of rim lays down one full circumference of road. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:One rotation moves the wheel forward by 2 pi R|id=key-1>> That single fact, one rotation equals two pi R of road, is the heart of rolling. Burn it in. <<PAUSE:short>> Now watch the wheel from the side of the road. Is it spinning in place, or sliding straight forward? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It is doing both at once. <<TRACE:centre-path>> The centre of the wheel glides forward in a perfectly straight line, never going up or down. <<WRITE_TEXT:Centre moves straight, rim loops|id=text-1>> But <<FOCUS:rim-point>> the painted point on the rim does something wild. Watch <<TRACE:rim-path>> the path it traces as the wheel rolls one full turn. <<UNFOCUS>> It draws a series of arching loops, called a cycloid. The rim point is not going in a circle and not going in a straight line, because it is being spun and carried forward at the same time. <<PAUSE:short>> Here is the strangest detail. Look at <<FOCUS:contact-point>> the point touching the road right now. <<UNFOCUS>> At the very instant it touches, that point is momentarily standing still. <<SECTION:The rolling relation|id=sec-2>> So how do the spinning and the sliding connect? In one full turn the wheel sweeps an angle of two pi and the centre travels two pi R, so distance forward is just radius times the angle turned. The distance the wheel moves forward equals the radius times the angle it has rotated through. <<WRITE_EQUATION:x = R\,\theta|id=eq-1|boxed>> Here's an example from the chapter on rolling. We have a wheel of radius R in pure rolling, turning with angular velocity omega, and we want the velocity of three special points: the contact point at the bottom, the centre of mass, and the topmost point. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In pure rolling, find the velocity of the contact point, the centre, and the topmost point.|id=ex-q-1>> The speed of the centre equals the radius times how fast the wheel is spinning. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v = R\,\omega|id=eq-2|boxed>> We start with the pure rolling condition. In pure rolling the wheel does not slip, so the point touching the ground is momentarily at rest. That means the velocity of the contact point is zero. <<WRITE_STEP:Pure rolling: velocity of contact point = 0|id=ex-step-1-1>> The centre of mass sits <<FOCUS:centre-point+contact-point>> a distance R above that contact point, so its velocity is omega times R. <<WRITE_STEP:v of centre = omega times R|id=ex-step-1-2>> Finally, <<FOCUS:rim-point>> the topmost point is a distance two R from the contact point, so it moves at two omega R, which is exactly twice the velocity of the centre. <<WRITE_STEP:v of topmost point = 2 omega R = 2 times v of centre|id=ex-step-1-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the answer: the contact point has zero velocity, the centre moves at omega times R, and the topmost point moves at two omega R, twice the velocity of the centre. <<WRITE_ANSWER:contact = 0, centre = omega R, top = 2 omega R = 2 v of centre|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. A wheel of radius r rolls without slipping. The wheel spins with angular velocity omega, while the car moves forward with velocity v. Because this is pure rolling, the condition v equals omega times r holds. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: A wheel of radius r rolls without slipping; angular velocity omega, car velocity v, with v = omega r. Find the velocity of the contact point with respect to the road.|id=ex-q-1>> We use relative velocity. The velocity of the lowest particle with respect to the road equals its velocity with respect to the car plus the velocity of the car with respect to the road. <<WRITE_STEP:v(contact, road) = v(contact, car) + v(car, road)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we plug in the pieces. The contact point sits at the bottom of the wheel, so its velocity with respect to the car is minus omega times r, pointing backward. The velocity of the car with respect to the road is v, pointing forward. <<WRITE_STEP:v(contact, road) = -omega r + v|id=ex-step-1-2>> Since pure rolling gives v equals omega times r, the minus omega r and the plus v cancel exactly. The sum equals zero. <<WRITE_STEP:= -omega r + omega r = 0|id=ex-step-1-3>> And the answer is that the velocity of the contact point with respect to the road is zero. The point touching the ground is instantaneously at rest. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v(contact, road) = 0|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose the driver pushes the car faster, so that v is greater than omega r. The wheel can no longer grip the road cleanly, and we want to know what happens at the contact point. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: When v is greater than omega r, what motion does the wheel undergo at the contact point?|id=ex-q-1>> We find the velocity of the contact point with respect to the road by adding two pieces: the velocity of the contact point relative to the car, which is minus omega r, and the velocity of the car relative to the road, which is plus v. <<WRITE_STEP:velocity of contact w.r.t. road = (-omega r) + v|id=ex-step-1-1>> Since v is greater than omega r, this sum, minus omega r plus v, is greater than zero. A positive value means the contact point moves forward relative to the road, so this is rolling with forward slipping. <<WRITE_ANSWER:v_contact,road = -omega r + v > 0  =>  rolling with forward slipping|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Suppose the forward velocity v of the center is less than omega r, that is, less than the angular velocity times the radius. We want to know what's happening at the contact point. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: If v is less than omega r, what happens at the point of contact?|id=ex-q-1>> We start by writing the velocity of the contact point with respect to the road. It's the translational velocity v plus the contact-point velocity due to rotation, which points backward as minus omega r. So the velocity of contact with respect to the road equals minus omega r plus v. <<WRITE_STEP:velocity of contact with respect to road = minus omega r plus v|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now since v is less than omega r, the quantity minus omega r plus v is less than zero. A negative contact velocity means the particles at the contact rub the road backward. So the answer is: this is rolling with backward slipping. <<WRITE_ANSWER:velocity of contact with respect to road = minus omega r plus v, which is less than zero, so this is rolling with backward slipping|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_STEP:speed of centre = R times spin rate|id=step-1>> Divide both by the time taken, and you get a beautifully simple link: the speed of the centre equals the radius times how fast the wheel spins. <<PAUSE:short>> So a rolling wheel is never just spinning and never just sliding. It is the two woven together, and that single idea explains everything from bicycles to gears to the wheels under a train.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_18>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_18:rolling_wheel>> A wheel rolls down a hill. It's <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> spinning around its own center AND it's <<FOCUS:forward-arrow>> gliding forward at the same time — so how much energy does it actually carry? <<PAUSE:long>> <<FOCUS:center-mark>> Watch the center of the wheel. As the wheel rolls, that single point <<FOCUS:forward-arrow>> glides smoothly forward across the road. <<UNFOCUS>> But the wheel is also turning. Every part of it <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> whirls around that center, again and again. <<WRITE_TEXT:Two motions at once: spin + glide|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the wheel is doing two things at once, and any honest energy count has to include both of them. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's the trick the physicist uses: ride along with the center of mass. In that travelling frame, the center sits still and the body is doing nothing but pure spinning. If you stand on the ground instead, every particle's velocity is just <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> its spinning velocity plus the <<FOCUS:forward-arrow>> forward velocity of the center. <<UNFOCUS>> So how do those combine into one clean energy? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> When you square that combined velocity and add it up over every particle, the cross-term — the part that mixes spin and glide — sums to exactly zero, because the center of mass doesn't move within its own frame. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Energy splits in two|id=sec-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:K = spin energy about center + forward energy of whole mass|id=key-1>> What's left are two separate pieces that simply add: <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> the spin energy about the center, plus the <<FOCUS:forward-arrow>> straight-line energy of the whole mass moving forward. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The total energy is the spin energy about the center of mass added to the straight-line energy of the whole mass moving forward. <<WRITE_EQUATION:K = \tfrac{1}{2} I_{cm}\,\omega^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} M v_0^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> The first piece is one half times the moment of inertia about the center times the angular velocity squared. The second is one half times the total mass times the center's speed squared. Now here's what makes rolling special. <<FOCUS:contact-point>> Look at the contact point — the place where the wheel meets the road. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v = R\omega|id=eq-roll>> For pure rolling, that contact point is momentarily still, which locks the spin and the glide together: <<FOCUS:forward-arrow+spin-arrow>> the forward speed equals the radius times the angular velocity. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> For pure rolling, since the forward speed equals the radius times the angular velocity, the two pieces combine into one expression written purely in terms of the spin. <<WRITE_EQUATION:K = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(I_{cm} + MR^2\right)\omega^2|id=eq-2|boxed>> Substitute that lock-in, and the two pieces fold into one tidy expression in terms of spin alone — the energy of the whole rolling motion about the contact line. <<WRITE_KEY:Rolling KE = spin about center + glide of center, locked by v = R-omega|id=key-2>> So remember this: a rolling body's energy is <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> spin about its center plus the <<FOCUS:forward-arrow>> forward energy of its mass — and rolling ties those two together through v equals R times omega. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_19>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_19:rolling_wheel_split>> A wheel rolling down a road is doing two things at once — <<FOCUS:spin-arc>> it spins around its own centre, and <<FOCUS:v0-vector>> the whole thing travels down the road. <<UNFOCUS>> So how much angular momentum does it really carry about a fixed point in the lab? <<PAUSE:long>> Let's plant a fixed point in the lab and <<FOCUS:origin-O>> call it O. Angular momentum about O means we add up, <<FOCUS:piece-mi>> for every tiny piece of the wheel, its mass times its position cross its velocity. <<SECTION:Splitting position and velocity|id=sec-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the clever trick. The position of any little piece can be written as two arrows added together. <<WRITE_TEXT:position = r naught + r relative to c.m.|id=text-1>> One arrow goes <<TRACE:r0-vector>> from O to the centre of mass, that's r naught. The second goes from the centre of mass <<TRACE:ri-cm-vector>> out to the little piece, that's r i relative to the centre of mass. And we do exactly the same with velocity — the velocity of each piece is the velocity of the centre of mass, <<FOCUS:v0-vector>> v naught, plus the piece's velocity as seen from the centre of mass. <<UNFOCUS>> We write each piece's position as r naught plus its position from the centre of mass, and each piece's velocity the same way, then put both into the angular momentum sum. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{L} = \sum_i m_i\,(\vec{r}_{i,cm} + \vec{r}_0) \times (\vec{v}_{i,cm} + \vec{v}_0)|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<SECTION:What happens when you multiply out|id=sec-2>> Now substitute both split-up arrows into the sum and expand the cross product. You get four terms instead of one. Two of those four terms are mixed — they pair the centre-of-mass position with the relative velocity, and the other way round. Here's the magic: both of them vanish. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Why would they just vanish? Because each mixed term contains the sum of mass times position measured from the centre of mass itself — and the centre of mass, measured from where it sits, is exactly at the origin. Add up mass times position there and you get zero. <<PAUSE:short>> The same reasoning kills the other mixed term, because the total momentum measured in the centre-of-mass frame is also zero. The cross terms are gone. <<PAUSE:short>> Adding up mass times position measured from the centre of mass gives zero, and so does adding up mass times velocity in that frame — that's what makes the mixed terms disappear. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\sum_i m_i \vec{r}_{i,cm} = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \sum_i m_i \vec{v}_{i,cm} = 0|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_KEY:L total = L spin + M r naught cross v naught|id=key-1>> So only two terms survive, and they tell a beautiful story. The total angular momentum splits cleanly into a spin part plus an orbit part. <<PAUSE:short>> What's left is the spin about the centre of mass plus the angular momentum of all the mass treated as a single point at the centre of mass. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{L} = \vec{L}_{cm} + M\,\vec{r}_0 \times \vec{v}_0|id=eq-3|boxed>> The first piece is the angular momentum the wheel has from <<FOCUS:spin-arc>> spinning about its own centre — exactly what you'd measure riding along with the centre of mass. The second piece treats the whole wheel as a single point — all its mass <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass>> crammed onto the centre of mass, <<FOCUS:v0-vector+origin-O>> moving with velocity v naught about O. <<UNFOCUS>> Spin plus orbit, that's the whole answer. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_20>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_20:rolling_sphere_forces>> Roll a ball across a table and it always slows down and stops. Simple, right? But there's a hidden trap here that fools almost everyone. <<SECTION:The three forces|id=sec-1>> Let's be careful and draw every force on the ball. First, its <<FOCUS:weight-arrow>> weight pulls straight down through the centre. Second, the table <<FOCUS:normal-arrow>> pushes back up with the normal force. And third, there's <<FOCUS:friction-arrow>> friction right at the point where the ball touches the table. Now the ball is <<FOCUS:velocity-arrow>> moving to the right and slowing down, so <<FOCUS:friction-arrow>> friction must point backward, to the left, opposing the motion. <<UNFOCUS>> That feels completely natural. But watch what that backward friction does to the spinning. It <<FOCUS:friction-arrow>> pushes left at the very bottom of the ball. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the puzzle: a backward shove at the bottom is exactly what makes a ball roll faster, not slower. That friction gives a clockwise torque that should speed the spin up. So why doesn't the ball spin faster forever? <<PAUSE:long>> <<WRITE_KEY:Friction speeds the spin up, so it can't be what stops the sphere|id=key-1>> So friction can't be the villain. If anything, it would keep the ball rolling. We need another torque, a braking one, that we haven't drawn yet. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The contact is not a point|id=sec-2>> The trick is an assumption we made without noticing. We drew the ball <<FOCUS:center-line>> touching the table at a single point. In reality, both the ball and the table squash a little, and they <<FOCUS:contact-area>> touch over a small area. <<PAUSE:short>> And here's the payoff: as the ball rolls forward, its front edge presses into the table harder than its trailing edge. <<UNFOCUS>> So the upward push isn't centred underneath, it bunches up toward the front. <<WRITE_TEXT:Normal force shifts forward, off the centre line|id=text-1>> That means the normal force no longer points straight up through the centre. It's <<FOCUS:normal-shift+normal-arrow>> shifted forward, to the right of the centre. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:normal-arrow>> An upward force in front of the centre twists the ball the other way, an anticlockwise torque. <<UNFOCUS>> That is the genuine brake on the spinning. <<PAUSE:short>> So the real answer is delightfully sneaky. A rolling sphere slows down because it deforms the surface, the normal force shifts forward, and that off-centre push creates the torque that quietly steals its spin away.
