segments.raw_narration: Flip on a ceiling fan and the blades whirl faster and faster, yet the center never moves. That is a genuine puzzle.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:fan-center>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_3:fan_spinning>> Flip on a ceiling fan and the blades whirl faster and faster, yet the center never moves. That is a genuine puzzle. <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Watch the hub. It is bolted to the ceiling, so it stays perfectly still while the blades pick up speed around it.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> Watch the hub. It is bolted to the ceiling, so it stays perfectly still while the blades pick up speed around it. <<TRACE:spin-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:spin speeding up = angular acceleration|id=text-1>>This speeding up of the spin has a name. We call it angular acceleration.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_TEXT:spin speeding up = angular acceleration|id=text-1>>This speeding up of the spin has a name. We call it angular acceleration. <<POINT:spin-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: Now here is the key observation. If the center of the fan stays at rest, then the outside forces on the fan must all add up to exactly zero.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:fan-center>> Now here is the key observation. If the center of the fan stays at rest, then the outside forces on the fan must all add up to exactly zero. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Angular acceleration possible even with zero net force|id=key-1>>So we have discovered something surprising: you can have angular acceleration even when the total external force is zero.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Angular acceleration possible even with zero net force|id=key-1>>So we have discovered something surprising: you can have angular acceleration even when the total external force is zero. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Look at how that works. Push the top blade one way, and an equal push sends the bottom blade the opposite way. The two forces cancel.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:force-up>> Look at how that works. Push the top blade one way, and an equal push sends the bottom blade the opposite way. The two forces cancel. <<POINT:force-up>>

segments.raw_narration: Their sum is zero, so the center never budges, but both pushes still drive the blades around the same way.
segments.text_with_markers: Their sum is zero, so the center never budges, but both pushes still drive the blades around the same way. <<POINT:force-down>>

segments.raw_narration: But now flip the question around. If zero net force can spin a fan, why must you bother switching it on at all?
segments.text_with_markers: <<UNFOCUS>> But now flip the question around. If zero net force can spin a fan, why must you bother switching it on at all? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Why does a wheel on the floor not just start spinning the instant you wish it would? Why must your muscles do work?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:fan-center>> Why does a wheel on the floor not just start spinning the instant you wish it would? Why must your muscles do work?

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:No angular acceleration without an external force|id=key-2>>Here is the resolution: you cannot get angular acceleration without an external force. The fan needs that push.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:force-up>> <<WRITE_KEY:No angular acceleration without an external force|id=key-2>>Here is the resolution: you cannot get angular acceleration without an external force. The fan needs that push. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So both things are true at once. Net force can be zero, yet force must still be present. What really matters is not where the forces point, but how they twist.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> So both things are true at once. Net force can be zero, yet force must still be present. What really matters is not where the forces point, but how they twist. <<TRACE:spin-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:torque = the twisting effect of a force|id=text-2>>That twisting effect is the real cause of angular acceleration, and it has a name we meet next: torque.

segments.raw_narration: Push a door right next to its hinge, as hard as you like, and it barely moves. Push at the far edge with one finger, and it swings open.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:door-line>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_4:door_torque_topview>> Push a door right next to its hinge, as hard as you like, and it barely moves. Push at the far edge with one finger, and it swings open.

segments.raw_narration: Same door, same muscles — so why does where you push change everything? <<SECTION:Turning effect of a force|id=sec-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: Same door, same muscles — so why does where you push change everything? <<SECTION:Turning effect of a force|id=sec-1>> <<POINT:hinge-axis>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: The secret is the distance from the hinge. Here is the arrow from the hinge to the spot where you push — call it r.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:position-vector-r>> The secret is the distance from the hinge. Here is the arrow from the hinge to the spot where you push — call it r. <<TRACE:position-vector-r>>

segments.raw_narration: Now here is your push, the force F, pointing straight off the face of the door.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:force-vector-f>> Now here is your push, the force F, pointing straight off the face of the door. <<TRACE:force-vector-f>>

segments.raw_narration: The turning effect — physicists call it torque — grows when r is longer and when your push is more perpendicular to the door. <<WRITE_TEXT:torque = turning effect of a force|id=text-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:torque-arrow>> The turning effect — physicists call it torque — grows when r is longer and when your push is more perpendicular to the door. <<WRITE_TEXT:torque = turning effect of a force|id=text-1>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Watch what happens if you push straight along the door, toward the hinge instead — this faded arrow. The door doesn't turn at all, even though you're pushing hard.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:force-along-door>> Watch what happens if you push straight along the door, toward the hinge instead — this faded arrow. The door doesn't turn at all, even though you're pushing hard. <<TRACE:force-along-door>>

segments.raw_narration: So direction matters as much as distance, and there's one clean operation that captures both at once.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:position-vector-r>> So direction matters as much as distance, and there's one clean operation that captures both at once.

segments.raw_narration: Torque equals the position vector r crossed with the force F, a vector pointing along the axis of the spin.
segments.text_with_markers: Torque equals the position vector r crossed with the force F, a vector pointing along the axis of the spin. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{\Gamma} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Torque is r crossed with F|id=key-1>>We write the torque as r crossed with F — the cross product. It points along the axis the door turns about, and its length measures the turning strength.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:torque-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Torque is r crossed with F|id=key-1>>We write the torque as r crossed with F — the cross product. It points along the axis the door turns about, and its length measures the turning strength. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: The cross product hides a beautiful shortcut. Drop a perpendicular from the hinge onto the line of your push — this dashed distance.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:perp-distance>> The cross product hides a beautiful shortcut. Drop a perpendicular from the hinge onto the line of your push — this dashed distance. <<TRACE:perp-distance>>

segments.raw_narration: The size of the torque is r times F times the sine of the angle between them, which is just the force times the perpendicular distance to the axis.
segments.text_with_markers: The size of the torque is r times F times the sine of the angle between them, which is just the force times the perpendicular distance to the axis. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = r F \sin\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = F \times d_{\perp}|id=eq-1>>The torque is simply your force times that perpendicular distance — push farther out, or more squarely, and the perpendicular distance grows.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:perp-distance>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:\Gamma = F \times d_{\perp}|id=eq-1>>The torque is simply your force times that perpendicular distance — push farther out, or more squarely, and the perpendicular distance grows. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Now a subtle question: to measure torque you needed an origin on the axis. Would picking a different point on the hinge line give a different answer?
segments.text_with_markers: Now a subtle question: to measure torque you needed an origin on the axis. Would picking a different point on the hinge line give a different answer? <<POINT:hinge-axis>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: It does not. Slide your origin anywhere up or down the axis and the extra piece you add points along the axis, contributing nothing to the spin — so the torque about the line stays exactly the same.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:hinge-axis>> It does not. Slide your origin anywhere up or down the axis and the extra piece you add points along the axis, contributing nothing to the spin — so the torque about the line stays exactly the same. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: So torque is r crossed with F: push far from the axis and push perpendicular for the strongest turn — and you're free to choose any convenient origin on the axis.

Torque equals the position vector r crossed with the force F, a vector pointing along the axis of the spin. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{\Gamma} = \vec{r} \times \vec{F}|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:torque-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Torque is r crossed with F|id=key-1>>We write the torque as r crossed with F — the cross product. segments.raw_narration: Why do you lean your bike into a turn? Try staying bolt upright through a sharp corner, and you'll feel yourself toppling outward.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:cyclist-body>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_7:cyclist_lean_forces>> Why do you lean your bike into a turn? Try staying bolt upright through a sharp corner, and you'll feel yourself toppling outward. <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Why leaning is forced|id=sec-1>>To travel in a circle, something must constantly pull you toward the centre, otherwise you'd shoot off in a straight line. On a flat road, that inward pull can only come from one place: the friction where your tyres grip the ground.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:friction-vector>> <<SECTION:Why leaning is forced|id=sec-1>>To travel in a circle, something must constantly pull you toward the centre, otherwise you'd shoot off in a straight line. On a flat road, that inward pull can only come from one place: the friction where your tyres grip the ground. <<POINT:friction-vector>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Friction at the tyres supplies the inward force|id=text-1>>So friction at the contact point is your inward force. Without leaning, you'd ride upright and friction would still be there, pulling your wheels inward.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:contact-point>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Friction at the tyres supplies the inward force|id=text-1>>So friction at the contact point is your inward force. Without leaning, you'd ride upright and friction would still be there, pulling your wheels inward.

segments.raw_narration: Here's the problem with staying upright: that inward friction acts down at the road, but your body's weight acts up at the centre of mass. Those two together would twist you, and you'd tip over the outside.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass>> Here's the problem with staying upright: that inward friction acts down at the road, but your body's weight acts up at the centre of mass. Those two together would twist you, and you'd tip over the outside. <<POINT:centre-of-mass>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Lean inward so friction can curve your path|id=key-1>>So you lean inward. To go round a flat curve, a cyclist must lean so the ground's friction can supply the inward force that bends his path into a circle.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:lean-angle>> <<WRITE_KEY:Lean inward so friction can curve your path|id=key-1>>So you lean inward. To go round a flat curve, a cyclist must lean so the ground's friction can supply the inward force that bends his path into a circle. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Balancing the torques|id=sec-2>>Now let's find the exact angle. Look at the contact point A where the tyre meets the road. Both the normal force and the friction act right through A, so about that point they create no twist at all.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:normal-vector>> <<SECTION:Balancing the torques|id=sec-2>>Now let's find the exact angle. Look at the contact point A where the tyre meets the road. Both the normal force and the friction act right through A, so about that point they create no twist at all. <<POINT:normal-vector>>

segments.raw_narration: That leaves only two forces that can twist you about A: your weight pulling down, and the inward force needed for the circle. If your lean is correct, their twists exactly cancel, and you ride steadily.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:weight-vector>> That leaves only two forces that can twist you about A: your weight pulling down, and the inward force needed for the circle. If your lean is correct, their twists exactly cancel, and you ride steadily. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Working in the rotating frame, the system is at rest, so the total external force and total external torque must both be zero. Two forces act through the body: the weight, equal to M times g, acting downward, and the centrifugal force, equal to M times v squared divided by r, acting outward through the center of mass. <<WRITE_STEP:Weight = Mg (downward); Centrifugal force = Mv^2/r (outward)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

segments.raw_narration: Now we take torques about the contact point A. The normal force N and the friction f both pass through A, so their torques about A are zero. segments.raw_narration: The torque of the weight about A is M g times the distance A D, in the clockwise direction. The torque of the centrifugal force is M v squared over r times the distance C D, in the anticlockwise direction. <<WRITE_STEP:Torque of weight = Mg(AD) clockwise; Torque of centrifugal force = (Mv^2/r)(CD) anticlockwise|id=ex-step-1-3>>

segments.raw_narration: For rotational equilibrium the two torques are equal, so M g times A D equals M v squared over r times C D. Dividing, the ratio A D over C D equals v squared over r g, and that ratio is exactly the tangent of the lean angle theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Mg(AD) = \frac{Mv^2}{r}(CD) \;\Rightarrow\; \tan\theta = \frac{AD}{CD} = \frac{v^2}{rg}|id=ex-eq-1>>
segments.text_with_markers: For rotational equilibrium the two torques are equal, so M g times A D equals M v squared over r times C D. Dividing, the ratio A D over C D equals v squared over r g, and that ratio is exactly the tangent of the lean angle theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Mg(AD) = \frac{Mv^2}{r}(CD) \;\Rightarrow\; \tan\theta = \frac{AD}{CD} = \frac{v^2}{rg}|id=ex-eq-1>>

segments.raw_narration: And so the answer is that the cyclist bends at an angle theta whose tangent equals v squared divided by r times g — that is, theta equals the inverse tangent of v squared over r g, measured from the vertical. <<WRITE_ANSWER:theta = arctan(v^2 / rg) from the vertical|id=ex-ans-1>>

segments.raw_narration: The tangent of the lean angle equals v squared over r times g. Go faster, or take a tighter bend, and you must lean further in.

segments.raw_narration: A spinning wheel isn't going anywhere — its center sits perfectly still. So where on earth is its energy hiding?

segments.raw_narration: Here's the trick: a solid body is really just a huge crowd of tiny particles, all glued together, all spinning around the same axis.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:rotation-axis>> Here's the trick: a solid body is really just a huge crowd of tiny particles, all glued together, all spinning around the same axis. <<POINT:rotation-axis>>

segments.raw_narration: Pick out just one of them — this little particle here, sitting a distance r sub i from the axis.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:radius-i>> Pick out just one of them — this little particle here, sitting a distance r sub i from the axis. <<TRACE:radius-i>>

segments.raw_narration: As the body turns, this particle isn't standing still at all — it races around its own little circle.
segments.text_with_markers: As the body turns, this particle isn't standing still at all — it races around its own little circle. <<TRACE:circle-path-i>>

segments.raw_narration: And we already know its speed. For circular motion, the linear speed is simply the angular speed omega times the radius, so v sub i equals omega times r sub i.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:velocity-i>> And we already know its speed. For circular motion, the linear speed is simply the angular speed omega times the radius, so v sub i equals omega times r sub i.

segments.text_with_markers: The linear speed of any particle equals the angular speed times its distance from the axis. <<WRITE_EQUATION:v_i = \omega r_i|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_STEP:Particle KE = one half m v squared, with v = omega r|id=step-1>>So this one particle carries kinetic energy one half times its mass times its speed squared — and since the speed is omega times r sub i, that becomes one half m sub i times omega squared times r sub i squared.
segments.text_with_markers: <<WRITE_STEP:Particle KE = one half m v squared, with v = omega r|id=step-1>>So this one particle carries kinetic energy one half times its mass times its speed squared — and since the speed is omega times r sub i, that becomes one half m sub i times omega squared times r sub i squared.

segments.raw_narration: So one particle's kinetic energy is one half its mass times omega squared times its radius squared.
segments.text_with_markers: So one particle's kinetic energy is one half its mass times omega squared times its radius squared. <<WRITE_EQUATION:KE_i = \tfrac{1}{2} m_i \omega^2 r_i^2|id=eq-2|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: When you spin a bike wheel by pushing the pedal harder and harder, you're pouring energy into it every single second — and there's a beautifully simple way to count exactly how fast.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:wheel-body>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_13:spinning_wheel_torque>> When you spin a bike wheel by pushing the pedal harder and harder, you're pouring energy into it every single second — and there's a beautifully simple way to count exactly how fast.

segments.raw_narration: Here's our wheel, free to turn about this fixed axis, and a torque is acting on it, twisting it the same way it's already spinning.
segments.text_with_markers: Here's our wheel, free to turn about this fixed axis, and a torque is acting on it, twisting it the same way it's already spinning. <<POINT:torque-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: Because that torque produces angular acceleration, the wheel spins faster and faster, and as it speeds up its rotational kinetic energy keeps climbing.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:omega-arrow>> Because that torque produces angular acceleration, the wheel spins faster and faster, and as it speeds up its rotational kinetic energy keeps climbing.

segments.raw_narration: Now think back to straight-line motion: when a force makes something speed up, the rate at which its kinetic energy grows is exactly the power being delivered to it.
segments.text_with_markers: Now think back to straight-line motion: when a force makes something speed up, the rate at which its kinetic energy grows is exactly the power being delivered to it.

segments.raw_narration: So here's the honest question — if energy is flowing into this wheel every second, how fast is it actually arriving?

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Power from a torque|id=sec-1>>The rate of increase of kinetic energy IS the power, so let's just differentiate the rotational kinetic energy and see what falls out.
segments.text_with_markers: <<SECTION:Power from a torque|id=sec-1>>The rate of increase of kinetic energy IS the power, so let's just differentiate the rotational kinetic energy and see what falls out.

segments.raw_narration: The rotational kinetic energy is one half I omega squared, and when we ask how fast that changes, the moment of inertia I stays constant and only omega is changing.
segments.text_with_markers: The rotational kinetic energy is one half I omega squared, and when we ask how fast that changes, the moment of inertia I stays constant and only omega is changing.

segments.raw_narration: Differentiating gives I times omega times the rate of change of omega — and that rate of change of omega is just the angular acceleration alpha.
segments.text_with_markers: Differentiating gives I times omega times the rate of change of omega — and that rate of change of omega is just the angular acceleration alpha.

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_KEY:Power delivered: P = Gamma times omega|id=key-1>>But I times alpha is simply the torque Gamma, so the power is torque times angular velocity, P equals Gamma times omega — that's our answer.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Power delivered: P = Gamma times omega|id=key-1>>But I times alpha is simply the torque Gamma, so the power is torque times angular velocity, P equals Gamma times omega — that's our answer. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: The power is the rate of change of one half I omega squared, which works out to I times omega times alpha, and since I times alpha is the torque, it equals torque times angular velocity.
segments.text_with_markers: The power is the rate of change of one half I omega squared, which works out to I times omega times alpha, and since I times alpha is the torque, it equals torque times angular velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P = \frac{dK}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\right) = I\omega\alpha = \Gamma\omega|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: Look how clean that is: the power delivered by a torque is just the torque multiplied by the angular velocity, the perfect mirror of force times velocity in straight-line motion.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:omega-arrow>> Look how clean that is: the power delivered by a torque is just the torque multiplied by the angular velocity, the perfect mirror of force times velocity in straight-line motion. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Work done by a torque|id=sec-2>>Now, power is work done per second, so in a tiny slice of time the little bit of work is power times that time, which is Gamma times omega times d t.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:rim-point>> <<SECTION:Work done by a torque|id=sec-2>>Now, power is work done per second, so in a tiny slice of time the little bit of work is power times that time, which is Gamma times omega times d t.

segments.raw_narration: But omega times d t is just the small angle the wheel turns through, d theta — so each small bit of work is simply torque times the angle turned.
segments.text_with_markers: But omega times d t is just the small angle the wheel turns through, d theta — so each small bit of work is simply torque times the angle turned. <<TRACE:rim-point>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: In a tiny turn, the work done is the torque times the small angle the body rotates through.

segments.raw_narration: So how on earth do you do physics on a path like that? The trick is one of the most beautiful ideas in mechanics: don't fight the mess, split it.

segments.raw_narration: But here's the catch that worries a careful physicist. The frame riding with the center is accelerating, and our rotation law was proved only for inertial frames.

We have a wheel of radius R in pure rolling, turning with angular velocity omega, and we want the velocity of three special points: the contact point at the bottom, the centre of mass, and the topmost point. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: In pure rolling, find the velocity of the contact point, the centre, and the topmost point.|id=ex-q-1>>

segments.raw_narration: We start with the pure rolling condition. In pure rolling the wheel does not slip, so the point touching the ground is momentarily at rest. That means the velocity of the contact point is zero. <<WRITE_STEP:Pure rolling: velocity of contact point = 0|id=ex-step-1-1>> The centre of mass sits a distance R above that contact point, so its velocity is omega times R. <<WRITE_STEP:v of centre = omega times R|id=ex-step-1-2>>

segments.raw_narration: A wheel rolls down a hill. It's spinning around its own center AND it's gliding forward at the same time — so how much energy does it actually carry?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:wheel-body>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_18:rolling_wheel>> A wheel rolls down a hill. It's spinning around its own center AND it's gliding forward at the same time — so how much energy does it actually carry? <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: Watch the center of the wheel. As the wheel rolls, that single point glides smoothly forward across the road.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:forward-arrow>> Watch the center of the wheel. As the wheel rolls, that single point glides smoothly forward across the road. <<POINT:forward-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: But the wheel is also turning. Every part of it whirls around that center, again and again.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> But the wheel is also turning. Every part of it whirls around that center, again and again. <<TRACE:spin-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: <<WRITE_TEXT:Two motions at once: spin + glide|id=text-1>>So the wheel is doing two things at once, and any honest energy count has to include both of them.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:center-mark>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Two motions at once: spin + glide|id=text-1>>So the wheel is doing two things at once, and any honest energy count has to include both of them. <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: Here's the trick the physicist uses: ride along with the center of mass. In that travelling frame, the center sits still and the body is doing nothing but pure spinning.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:center-mark>> Here's the trick the physicist uses: ride along with the center of mass. In that travelling frame, the center sits still and the body is doing nothing but pure spinning.

segments.raw_narration: If you stand on the ground instead, every particle's velocity is just its spinning velocity plus the forward velocity of the center. So how do those combine into one clean energy?
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:forward-arrow>> If you stand on the ground instead, every particle's velocity is just its spinning velocity plus the forward velocity of the center. So how do those combine into one clean energy? <<POINT:forward-arrow>> <<PAUSE:long>>

segments.raw_narration: When you square that combined velocity and add it up over every particle, the cross-term — the part that mixes spin and glide — sums to exactly zero, because the center of mass doesn't move within its own frame.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:center-mark>> When you square that combined velocity and add it up over every particle, the cross-term — the part that mixes spin and glide — sums to exactly zero, because the center of mass doesn't move within its own frame.

segments.raw_narration: <<SECTION:Energy splits in two|id=sec-1>><<WRITE_KEY:K = spin energy about center + forward energy of whole mass|id=key-1>>What's left are two separate pieces that simply add: the spin energy about the center, plus the straight-line energy of the whole mass moving forward.
segments.text_with_markers: <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> <<SECTION:Energy splits in two|id=sec-1>><<WRITE_KEY:K = spin energy about center + forward energy of whole mass|id=key-1>>What's left are two separate pieces that simply add: the spin energy about the center, plus the straight-line energy of the whole mass moving forward. <<TRACE:spin-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>>

segments.raw_narration: The total energy is the spin energy about the center of mass added to the straight-line energy of the whole mass moving forward.
segments.text_with_markers: The total energy is the spin energy about the center of mass added to the straight-line energy of the whole mass moving forward. <<WRITE_EQUATION:K = \tfrac{1}{2} I_{cm}\,\omega^2 + \tfrac{1}{2} M v_0^2|id=eq-1|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: The first piece is one half times the moment of inertia about the center times the angular velocity squared. The second is one half times the total mass times the center's speed squared.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:forward-arrow>> The first piece is one half times the moment of inertia about the center times the angular velocity squared. The second is one half times the total mass times the center's speed squared. <<POINT:forward-arrow>>

segments.raw_narration: Now here's what makes rolling special. Look at the contact point — the place where the wheel meets the road.
segments.text_with_markers: <<FOCUS:contact-point>> Now here's what makes rolling special. Look at the contact point — the place where the wheel meets the road.

segments.raw_narration: For pure rolling, since the forward speed equals the radius times the angular velocity, the two pieces combine into one expression written purely in terms of the spin.
segments.text_with_markers: For pure rolling, since the forward speed equals the radius times the angular velocity, the two pieces combine into one expression written purely in terms of the spin. <<WRITE_EQUATION:K = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(I_{cm} + MR^2\right)\omega^2|id=eq-2|boxed>>

segments.raw_narration: Substitute that lock-in, and the two pieces fold into one tidy expression in terms of spin alone — the energy of the whole rolling motion about the contact line.

topics.topic_name: Rotation of a Rigid Body about a Given Fixed Line
topics.orig_book_content:
10.1 ROTATION OF A RIGID BODY 
    ABOUT A GIVEN FIXED LINE 
Take a rigid body like a plate or a ball or your
tennis racket or anything else present nearby and hold
it between your fingers at two points. Now keep these
two points fixed and then displace the body (try it with
any rigid body at hand).
Notice the kind of displacement you can produce.
In particular, notice that each particle of the rigid body
goes in a circle, the centre being on the line joining
the two fixed points between your finger tips. Let us
call this line the axis of rotation. In fact, the centre of
the circular path of a particle is at the foot of the
perpendicular from the particle to this axis. Different
particles move in different circles, the planes of all
these circles are parallel to each other, and the radii
depend on the distances of the particles from this axis.
The particles on the axis remain stationary, those close
to this line move on smaller circles and those far away
from this line move in larger circles. However, each
particle takes equal time to complete its circle.
Such a displacement of a rigid body in which a
given line is held fixed, is called rotation of the rigid
body about the given line. The line itself is called the
axis of rotation.
Examples : (1) Consider the door of your almirah.
When you open the door, the vertical line passing
through the hinges is held fixed and that is the axis
of rotation. Each point of the door describes a circle
with the centre at the foot of the perpendicular from
the particle on the axis. All these circles are horizontal
and thus perpendicular to the axis. 
(2) Consider the ceiling fan in your room. When it
is on, each point on its body goes in a circle. Locate
the centres of the circles traced by different particles
on the three blades of the fan and the body covering
the motor. All these centres lie on a vertical line
through the centre of the body. The fan rotates about
this vertical line.
(3) Look at the on–off switch on the front panel of
your gas stove in the kitchen. To put the gas on, you
push the switch a little, and then you rotate it. While
rotating, each particle of the switch moves on a circle.
Think about the centres of all such circles. They lie on
a straight line (generally horizontal, towards the
operator). This is the axis of rotation and the switch
rotates about this axis.
Sometimes the axis may not pass through the
body. Consider a record rotating on the turntable of a
record player. Suppose a fly is sitting on the record
near the rim. Look at the path of any particle of the
fly. It is a circle with the centre on the vertical line
through the centre of the record. The fly is “rotating
about this vertical line” (can you consider the fly as a
rigid body ?). The axis of rotation is lying completely
outside the fly.
If each particle of a rigid body moves in a circle,
with centres of all the circles on a straight line and
Figure 10.1

with planes of the circles perpendicular to this line,
we say that the body is rotating about this line. The
straight line itself is called the axis of rotation.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with a simple experiment you can do right now. Pick up any solid object near you — a plate, a ball, your tennis racket, even a book. Hold it between your fingers at two points, keep those two points fixed, and then try to move the object. What happens? You'll find you can't move it freely anymore. The only thing you can do is spin it. That spinning is exactly what we call rotation.

Now here's the beautiful part. When the body rotates this way, every single particle in it travels in a circle. The center of each of those circles sits on the straight line joining your two fingertips. We give that line a special name — the axis of rotation. To find the center of a particle's circle, you drop a straight perpendicular from that particle down to the axis, and the foot of that perpendicular is the center.

Notice that different particles trace different circles. The planes of all these circles are parallel to one another, and the size of each circle depends on how far that particle sits from the axis. Particles sitting right on the axis don't move at all — they stay still. Particles close to the axis sweep out small circles, and particles far away sweep out big circles. But here's the key insight that ties it all together: every particle, big circle or small, takes exactly the same time to complete one full loop. They all turn together as one.

Think about familiar examples. When you open the door of a cupboard, the vertical line through the hinges stays fixed — that's the axis. A ceiling fan spins about a vertical line through its center. The on-off knob on a gas stove rotates about a roughly horizontal line pointing toward you.

And here's something surprising: the axis doesn't have to pass through the body at all. Imagine a fly sitting near the edge of a spinning record on a turntable. The fly traces a circle whose center is on the vertical line through the record's center — but that line lies completely outside the fly. So a body can rotate about an axis that isn't even inside it. That's the full picture of what rotation about a fixed line really means.

events.text: Centre of each circle = foot of perpendicular to the axis
Radius = distance from axis
Each particle: centre on axis, same time per turn
Same angle, same time — that's why we measure rotation by angle

That last fact is why we'll soon describe spinning bodies not by distance, but by angle. <<PAUSE:short>>

10.2 KINEMATICS
Consider a rigid body rotating about a given fixed
line. Take this line as the Z-axis. Consider a particle
P of the body (figure 10.2). Look at its position P0 at
t = 0. Draw a perpendicular P0Q to the axis of rotation.
At time t, the particle moves to P. Let ∠PQP0 = θ. We
say that the particle P has rotated through an angle
θ. In fact, all the particles of the body have also rotated
through the same angle θ and so we say that the whole
rigid body has rotated through an angle θ. The
“angular position” of the body at time t is said to be
θ. If P has made a complete revolution on its circle,
every particle has done so and we say that the body
has rotated through an angle of 2π. So the rotation of
a rigid body is measured by the rotation of the line
QP from its initial position.
Now, suppose the angular position of the body at
time t is θ. During a time ∆t, it further rotates through
∆θ, so that its angular position becomes θ + ∆θ. The
average angular velocity during the time interval ∆t is
ω = ∆θ
∆t ⋅
The instantaneous angular velocity at time t is
               ω = dθ
dt ⋅
We associate the direction of the axis of rotation
with the angular velocity. If the body rotates
anticlockwise as seen through the axis, the angular
velocity is towards the viewer. If it rotates clockwise,
the angular velocity is away from the reader. It turns
out that the angular velocity adds like a vector and
hence it becomes a vector quantity. The magnitude of
angular velocity is called angular speed . However, we
shall continue to use the word angular velocity if the
direction of the axis is clear from the context. The SI
unit for angular velocity is radian/sec (rad/s). Quite
often the angular velocity is given in revolutions per
second (rev/s). The conversion in radian per second
may be made using 1 rev = 2 π radian.
If the body rotates through equal angles in equal
time intervals (irrespective of the smallness of the
intervals), we say that it rotates with uniform angular
velocity. In this case ω = dθ/dt = constant and thus
θ = ωt. If it is not the case, the body is said to be
rotationally “accelerated”. The angular acceleration is
defined as

As an example, think of your ceiling fan. Switch
on the fan. The fan rotates about a vertical line (axis).
The angle rotated by the fan in the first second is
small, that in the second second is larger, that in the
third second is still larger and so on. The fan, thus,
has an angular acceleration. The angular velocity
ω = dθ/dt  increases with time. Wait for about a couple
of minutes. The fan has now attained full speed. The
angle rotated in any time interval is now equal to the
angle rotated in the successive equal time interval. The
fan is rotating uniformly about the vertical axis. Now
switch off the fan. The angle rotated in any second is
smaller than the angle rotated in the previous second.
The angular velocity dω/dt decreases as time passes,
and finally it becomes zero when the fan stops. The
fan has an angular deceleration.
Given the axis of rotation, the body can rotate in
two directions. Looking through the axis, it may be
clockwise or anticlockwise. One has to define the
“positive” rotation. This may be defined according to
the convenience of the problem, but once decided, one
has to stick to the choice. The angular displacement,
angular velocity and the angular acceleration may
accordingly be positive or negative.
Notice the similarity between the motion of a
particle on a straight line and the rotation of a rigid
body about a fixed axis. The position of the particle
was decided by a single variable x, which could be
positive or negative according to the choice of the
positive direction of the X-axis. The rate of change of
position gave the velocity and the rate of change of
velocity gave the acceleration.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about a rigid body spinning around a fixed line, like a fan turning on its axis. Pick any single particle in that body. At the start, it sits in some position. A little later it has swung around to a new position, sweeping out an angle. We call that angle theta the angular position. Here's the beautiful part: every particle in the body sweeps out the very same angle, so we can describe the whole spinning body with just one number, theta. If a particle goes all the way around once, it has turned through two pi radians, a full revolution.

Now, how fast is it spinning? If the angle changes by a small amount delta theta during a small time delta t, the average angular velocity is delta theta divided by delta t. Make that time interval tiny and you get the instantaneous angular velocity, which we call omega. It has a direction too, along the axis of rotation, so it actually behaves like a vector. Its size alone is called angular speed. We measure it in radians per second, though sometimes it's given in revolutions per second, and you convert by remembering one revolution equals two pi radians.

If the body turns through equal angles in equal times, it spins uniformly, and theta is simply omega times t. If the spinning rate changes, the body has angular acceleration, which we call alpha, the rate of change of omega. When alpha stays constant, three lovely equations appear that look exactly like the ones for straight-line motion. Omega equals omega-naught plus alpha times t. Theta equals omega-naught times t plus one half alpha t squared. And omega squared equals omega-naught squared plus two alpha theta.

Think of your ceiling fan. When you switch it on, it turns a small angle in the first second, a bigger angle in the next, bigger still after that. That's angular acceleration. After a couple minutes it spins steadily, equal angles in equal times. Switch it off and it slows, angular deceleration, until it stops.

Notice how this mirrors a particle moving in a straight line, where one variable x told you position, its rate of change gave velocity, and that rate gave acceleration. Here theta plays the role of x.

Finally, link spinning to actual movement. A particle at distance r from the axis travels along a circle. The distance it moves is r times theta. Its linear speed along the tangent is r times omega, and its tangential acceleration is r times alpha. So particles farther from the axis move faster, while particles right on the axis don't move at all.

The motor of an engine is rotating about its axis with an angular velocity of 100 rev/minute. It comes to rest in 15 s, after being switched off. Assuming constant angular deceleration, calculate the number of revolutions made by it before coming to rest.

Solution : The initial angular velocity = 100 rev/minute = (10 π/3) rad/s. Final angular velocity = 0. Time interval = 15 s. Let the angular acceleration be α. Using the equation ω = ω0 + αt, we obtain α = (− 2π/9) rad/s². The angle rotated by the motor during this motion is θ = ω0 t + 1/2 αt² = (10π/3 rad/s)(15 s) − 1/2 (2π/9 rad/s²)(15 s)² = 25π rad = 12.5 revolutions. Hence the motor rotates through 12.5 revolutions before coming to rest.

10.3 ROTATIONAL DYNAMICS
When one switches a fan on, the centre of the fan
remains unmoved while the fan rotates with an
angular acceleration. As the centre of mass remains
at rest, the external forces acting on the fan must add
to zero. This means that one can have angular
acceleration even if the resultant external force is zero.
But then why do we need to switch on the fan in order
to start it ? If an angular acceleration may be achieved
with zero total external force, why does not a wheel
chair start rotating on the floor as soon as one wishes
it to do so. Why are we compelled to use our muscles
to set it into rotation ? In fact, one cannot have angular
acceleration without external forces.
What is then the relation between the force and
the angular acceleration ? We find that even if the
resultant external force is zero, we may have angular
acceleration. We also find that without applying an
external force we cannot have an angular acceleration.
What 
is 
responsible 
for 
producing 
angular
acceleration ? The answer is torque which we define
below.
168
Concepts of Physics
topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with something you've seen a thousand times: a ceiling fan. When you switch it on, notice what happens. The center of the fan stays put, right where it's mounted, but the blades spin up faster and faster. That speeding up of the spin is called angular acceleration. So here's a curious thing. The center of mass of the fan isn't going anywhere. And whenever the center of mass stays at rest, that tells us the outside forces pushing on the fan must all add up to zero. They cancel each other out. So we've just discovered something surprising: you can have angular acceleration, meaning the fan spins faster, even when the total external force is zero. That feels a little strange, doesn't it?

But now flip the question around. If you can get angular acceleration with zero net force, then why do you even need to switch the fan on? Why doesn't a wheelchair just start spinning on the floor the moment you wish it would? Why do you have to use your muscles to get a wheel turning? Clearly, you cannot get angular acceleration out of nothing. Something has to act. So we've landed on a puzzle with two halves that seem to contradict each other. On one hand, even when the net force is zero, you can still have angular acceleration. On the other hand, without any external force at all, you cannot get angular acceleration. Both of these are true.

Think about what this is really telling us. The simple total of the forces is not the thing that decides whether something starts to spin. If it were, the fan with its zero net force could never speed up, and yet it does. So plain force, by itself, is not the right quantity for rotation. There must be a different idea, a better measuring stick, that captures not just how hard you push, but where you push and in what direction relative to the axis. That quantity is called torque. Torque is what actually produces angular acceleration. It's the rotational cousin of force. Just as force causes ordinary acceleration in a straight line, torque causes angular acceleration in rotation. So this short section is really setting the stage. It's saying: hold on, force alone doesn't explain spinning, we need a new and more powerful concept, and that concept, which we'll build up carefully next, is torque.

Angular acceleration possible even with zero net force

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about torque, which is the turning effect of a force. When you push on a door, the door swings — but only if you push in the right spot and direction. Torque is the physics word for how effectively a force makes something rotate. We define the torque of a force about a point as the position vector r crossed with the force F. The cross product means torque is a vector pointing perpendicular to both r and F, and its size tells us how strong the turning effect is.

Now, when a rigid body spins about a fixed axis, we care about the component of that torque along the axis of rotation. A nice fact is that this torque about a line doesn't depend on where you put your origin, as long as you pick the origin somewhere on that line. So you can choose a convenient point.

There are a few special cases worth remembering. First, if the force is parallel to the axis, it produces zero torque about that axis. Second, if the line of the force crosses the axis, the torque is again zero — the force just pushes through the axis instead of turning it. Third, and this is the useful one, if the force is perpendicular to the axis but doesn't intersect it, then the torque equals the force times the length of the common perpendicular between the force's line of action and the axis. That common perpendicular is what we call the lever arm or moment arm. The farther from the axis you push, the bigger the torque. That's why door handles are placed far from the hinges.

We also choose a sign convention: torque that turns the body anticlockwise, as you view it down the axis, is taken as positive.

When many forces act, you find each torque separately and add them. Don't be tempted to add the forces first and then take one torque — that can give the wrong answer, because even forces that cancel can still produce a net turning effect.

Finally, this all builds toward a beautiful result that mirrors Newton's second law. Just as force equals mass times acceleration for straight-line motion, the total external torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration. The moment of inertia plays the role of mass for rotation, but unlike mass it depends on which axis you choose, because it adds up each particle's mass times the square of its distance from the axis.

10.6 BODIES IN EQUILIBRIUM
The centre of mass of a body remains in
equilibrium if the total external force acting on the
body is zero. This follows from the equation F = Ma.
Similarly, a body remains in rotational equilibrium if
the total external torque acting on the body is zero.
This follows from the equation Γ = Iα. Thus, if a body
remains at rest in an inertial frame, the total external
force acting on the body should be zero in any direction
and the total external torque should be zero about any
line.
We shall often find situations in which all the
forces acting on a body lie in a single plane as shown
in figure (10.10).
Let us take this plane as the X-Y plane. For
translational equilibrium
              ∑ Fx = 0
… (i)
   and          ∑ Fy = 0.
… (ii)
As all the forces are in the X-Y plane, Fz is
identically zero for each force and so ∑ Fz = 0 is
automatically 
satisfied. 
Now 
consider 
rotational
equilibrium. The torque of each force about the X-axis
is identically zero because either the force intersects
the axis or it is parallel to it. Similarly, the torque of
each force about the Y-axis is identically zero. In fact,
the torque about any line in the X-Y plane is zero.
Thus, the condition of rotational equilibrium is
               ∑ Γz = 0.
… (iii)
While taking torque about the Z-axis, the origin
can be chosen at any point in the plane of the forces.
That is, the torque can be taken about any line
perpendicular to the plane of the forces. In general,
the torque is different about different lines but it can
be shown that if the resultant force is zero, the total
torque about any line perpendicular to the plane of the
forces is equal. If it is zero about one such line, it will
be zero about all such lines.
If a body is placed on a horizontal surface, the
torque of the contact forces about the centre of mass
should be zero to maintain the equilibrium. This may
happen only if the vertical line through the centre of
mass cuts the base surface at a point within the
contact area or the area bounded by the contact points.
That is why a person leans in the opposite direction
when he or she lifts a heavy load in one hand.
The equilibrium of a body is called stable  if the
body tries to regain its equilibrium position after being
slightly displaced and released. It is called unstable if
it gets further displaced after being slightly displaced
and released. If it can stay in equilibrium even after
being slightly displaced and released, it is said to be
in neutral equilibrium.
In the case of stable equilibrium, the centre of
mass goes higher on being slightly displaced. For
unstable equilibrium it goes lower and for neutral
equilibrium it stays at the same height.
topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about what it really means for an object to be in equilibrium. There are actually two parts to this. The first is translational equilibrium, which just means the center of mass isn't accelerating. This comes straight from the idea that force equals mass times acceleration. If the total force on a body is zero, then the acceleration is zero, and the center of mass stays put or moves at a steady velocity. The second part is rotational equilibrium, which comes from the idea that torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration. If the total torque is zero, the body isn't gaining any spin. So for something to truly sit still, both conditions must hold: zero total force in every direction, and zero total torque about any line.

Now, very often all the forces acting on a body lie flat in one single plane. Picture them all lying in the X-Y plane like things on a tabletop. When that happens, life gets simpler. For the object not to slide, the forces left and right must cancel, and the forces up and down must cancel. Since nothing pokes out of the plane, the third direction takes care of itself automatically. For rotation, the only meaningful torque is the one that would spin the object within that plane, around the axis sticking straight out of it. So the rule becomes: the total torque about that perpendicular axis must be zero.

Here's a handy bonus. When you compute torque, you get to choose where to place your reference point. As long as the total force is already zero, the total torque comes out the same no matter which perpendicular line you pick. So if it's zero about one point, it's zero about all of them. That gives you freedom to pick the most convenient point.

Think about an object resting on the ground. To stay balanced, the vertical line dropping down through its center of mass must land inside its base. That's exactly why a person leans away from a heavy bag they're carrying in one hand. They shift their center of mass back over their feet.

Finally, equilibrium comes in flavors. Stable means a small nudge makes the object come back, and its center of mass rises when displaced. Unstable means a small nudge sends it tumbling, and its center of mass drops. Neutral means it just sits wherever you leave it, with the center of mass staying at the same height.

topics.our_understanding:
Have you ever noticed that when you ride a bicycle around a curve, you naturally lean into the turn? You don't push yourself upright — you tilt your body and your bike toward the center of the circle. This section explains exactly why that bending is necessary, and even tells us by how much you should lean.

Picture a cyclist riding at some speed v around a flat, circular road of radius r. The road is not banked, meaning it's perfectly horizontal, with no tilt built in. Now, to make sense of the situation, let's think of the cyclist and the bike together as one system, and we'll watch the whole thing from a rotating point of view — a frame that spins along with the cyclist. In this spinning frame, the cyclist appears to be standing still.

Here's the catch: whenever we work from a rotating frame, we have to add an imaginary outward push called the centrifugal force. Its size is the total mass times the speed squared divided by the radius, and it acts outward through the center of mass, away from the center of the circle. So now four forces act on our system. There's the weight pulling straight down, the normal force from the ground pushing up, the friction from the road acting at the point where the tire meets the ground, and that outward centrifugal force.

Since the cyclist is at rest in this frame, two things must be true: the forces balance, and the torques balance. The clever move is to take torques about the contact point where the wheel meets the road. Why there? Because both the normal force and friction pass right through that point, so their torques are zero — they drop out of the equation. That leaves just the weight and the centrifugal force fighting each other in a kind of twisting tug-of-war. The weight tries to topple the bike one way, the centrifugal force tries to topple it the other way.

Setting those two torques equal gives a beautiful result: the tangent of the lean angle equals the speed squared divided by the radius times g, where g is the acceleration due to gravity. So the faster you go, or the tighter your turn, the more you must lean. Notice the mass cancels out completely — a heavy rider and a light rider lean by exactly the same angle. That's the elegant heart of this whole idea.

Two forces act through the body: the weight, equal to M times g, acting downward, and the centrifugal force, equal to M times v squared divided by r, acting outward through the center of mass. <<WRITE_STEP:Weight = Mg (downward); Centrifugal force = Mv^2/r (outward)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we take torques about the contact point A. The normal force N and the friction f both pass through A, so their torques about A are zero. That leaves just the weight and the centrifugal force. <<WRITE_STEP:Torques about A: N and f pass through A, so their torques = 0|id=ex-step-1-2>> The torque of the weight about A is M g times the distance A D, in the clockwise direction. The torque of the centrifugal force is M v squared over r times the distance C D, in the anticlockwise direction. <<WRITE_STEP:Torque of weight = Mg(AD) clockwise; Torque of centrifugal force = (Mv^2/r)(CD) anticlockwise|id=ex-step-1-3>> For rotational equilibrium the two torques are equal, so M g times A D equals M v squared over r times C D. Dividing, the ratio A D over C D equals v squared over r g, and that ratio is exactly the tangent of the lean angle theta. <<WRITE_EQUATION:Mg(AD) = \frac{Mv^2}{r}(CD) \;\Rightarrow\; \tan\theta = \frac{AD}{CD} = \frac{v^2}{rg}|id=ex-eq-1>> And so the answer is that the cyclist bends at an angle theta whose tangent equals v squared divided by r times g — that is, theta equals the inverse tangent of v squared over r g, measured from the vertical. <<WRITE_ANSWER:theta = arctan(v^2 / rg) from the vertical|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:lean-angle>> The tangent of the lean angle equals v squared over r times g. Go faster, or take a tighter bend, and you must lean further in. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:cyclist-body>> <<WRITE_KEY:tan theta = v squared over r g|id=key-2>>So the next time you carve round a corner, remember: that lean isn't a trick, it's geometry. The tangent of theta equals v squared over r times g tells you exactly how hard to lean. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about angular momentum, which is the rotational cousin of ordinary linear momentum. You already know that a moving object has linear momentum, which is just its mass times its velocity. Angular momentum captures something similar, but it describes motion as seen from a particular point in space. Think about a particle moving through space, and pick some point O to watch it from. The angular momentum of that particle about O is defined as the cross product of two things: the position vector r, which points from O to the particle, and the linear momentum p, which is mass times velocity. We write this as l equals r cross p. Because it's a cross product, angular momentum is itself a vector, and its direction is perpendicular to both r and p.

Now, when you have many particles together, like a whole rotating body, the total angular momentum of the system is just the vector sum of the angular momenta of all the individual particles. You add them up one by one, keeping track of direction.

Here's a really useful way to picture the size of angular momentum. Imagine a particle of mass m moving with velocity v, and you're measuring its angular momentum about a point O. The magnitude works out to mass times velocity times r times the sine of the angle between r and v. And here's the neat trick: r times sine of theta is actually the perpendicular distance from O to the line along which the particle is moving. So angular momentum equals mass times velocity times that perpendicular distance. The farther the line of motion is from O, the bigger the angular momentum, even if the speed stays the same.

Finally, just like we defined torque about a line, we can define angular momentum about a line, say a line AB. You pick any point O on that line, work out r cross p about O, and then take the component of that vector that points along the line AB. That component is the angular momentum about the line. The beautiful thing here is that it doesn't matter which point on the line you choose — you get the same answer. This idea of angular momentum about a line becomes very powerful when we study spinning objects rotating about a fixed axis.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's connect two ideas you've already met: angular momentum and moment of inertia. We're going to discover a beautifully simple relationship that says angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular velocity.

Start with a single particle moving in a circle. Imagine a small ball whisking around a circular path of radius r, and at some instant it has speed v. We want its angular momentum about the axis that runs through the center of the circle. Here's a clever choice: since we can put the origin anywhere along that axis, let's put it right at the center of the circle. Now the position vector points straight outward along a radius, and the velocity vector points along the tangent, which is the direction the particle is actually moving. Those two directions are perpendicular to each other. When you take the cross product of position and momentum and the two are perpendicular, the size is simply mass times velocity times radius. And the direction of that cross product turns out to point right along the axis. So the angular momentum of this one particle about the axis is mass times velocity times radius.

Now let's build up to a whole rigid body spinning about some axis. Think of the body as made of many tiny particles. The whole thing rotates with one shared angular velocity, which we call omega. Take the i-th particle, going around a circle of radius r-i, with its circle lying flat, perpendicular to the spin axis. Its linear speed is its radius times omega, because everything farther from the axis moves faster. So its angular momentum is mass times velocity times radius, which becomes mass times radius times omega times radius, or mass times radius squared times omega.

Here's the key move: to get the angular momentum of the entire body, we just add up these contributions from every particle. When we do, omega is shared by all of them, so we can pull it out front, and what's left is the sum of each mass times its radius squared. But that sum is exactly the moment of inertia of the body about that axis. So angular momentum equals moment of inertia times omega.

Notice how neatly this mirrors linear motion, where momentum is mass times velocity. In rotation, moment of inertia plays the role of mass, and angular velocity plays the role of velocity. That parallel is why this little equation matters so much — it's the rotational twin of linear momentum.

Thus, the component of r × p along the axis is mvr itself.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about one of the most beautiful ideas in rotation: the conservation of angular momentum. Remember that angular momentum is a measure of how much rotation a system carries. For a single body spinning about a fixed axis, its angular momentum equals the moment of inertia times the angular velocity. Now here's the key result we want to build toward.

If you take the angular momentum of a whole system and watch how it changes over time, you find that its rate of change equals the total torque acting on the system. When you do the math carefully, summing over every particle, something wonderful happens to the internal forces. The particles in the body push and pull on each other, and those internal pushes create internal torques. But when you add them all up, the internal torques cancel out completely. They come in pairs that destroy each other. So what's left is only the torque from external forces. In words: the rate of change of angular momentum equals the total external torque.

Now think about what happens if there is no external torque at all. If the total external torque is zero, then the angular momentum simply cannot change. It stays constant. That's the principle of conservation of angular momentum, and it's one of the deepest rules in physics.

There's a simpler way to see this for a rigid body spinning about a fixed axis. Since angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular velocity, and the moment of inertia about that fixed axis stays the same, the rate of change of angular momentum equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration. And that equals the external torque. Same result.

Here's why this matters so much. Conservation laws let you solve problems without tracking every messy detail in between. Notice that if the moment of inertia of a system gets smaller, the angular velocity must get bigger to keep the product constant. That's exactly why a spinning ice skater speeds up when she pulls her arms in. No external torque acts on her, so her angular momentum is locked in. Pull the mass closer, spin faster. Push the mass out, spin slower. The total stays the same. Keep that picture in your mind, because it's the heart of countless problems in rotational mechanics.

Take both the wheels together as the system. The total angular momentum of the system before the coupling is Iω + 0 = Iω. When the second wheel is dropped into the axle, the two wheels slip on each other and exert forces of friction. The forces of friction have torques about the axis of rotation but these are torques of internal forces. No external torque is applied on the two-wheel system and hence the angular momentum of the system remains unchanged. If the common angular speed is ω′, the total angular momentum of the two-wheel system is 2Iω′ after the coupling. Thus, Iω = 2Iω′ or, ω′ = ω/2.

Their torques cancel. <<POINT:force-b-on-a>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:particle-a>> Now sum over every single pair in the body. The internal torques add up to zero, every push matched by its partner. Only the external torque survives. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So the rate of change of angular momentum equals only the total external torque. That is the payoff to our question: internal forces, however violent, can never change the spin of the whole system. The rate of change of angular momentum equals only the total external torque on the system. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\frac{d\vec{L}}{dt} = \vec{\Gamma}_{\text{ext}}|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<WRITE_KEY:External torque = 0 means L stays constant|id=key-1>>And here is the beautiful consequence. If the total external torque is zero, then the rate of change is zero, which means the angular momentum simply stays constant. <<PAUSE:short>> If the total external torque is zero, the angular momentum stays constant. <<WRITE_EQUATION:\vec{\Gamma}_{\text{ext}} = 0 \implies \vec{L} = \text{constant}|id=eq-3|boxed>> <<FOCUS:arms-out>> <<SECTION:Back to the skater|id=sec-3>>Now return to our skater. With her arms flung wide, her mass sits far from the axis, so her moment of inertia I is large and she spins gently. <<FOCUS:spin-axis>> The ice is nearly frictionless, so there is almost no external torque on her. That means her angular momentum, I times omega, must stay locked at the same value. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. A first wheel is rotating at an angular speed omega about its axle, which is kept vertical. Each wheel has the same moment of inertia I about that axis. A second identical wheel, initially at rest, is gently dropped onto the same axle, and the two begin rotating together. We want the common angular speed. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: First wheel spins at angular speed omega; identical wheel at rest dropped on same axle. Find common angular speed.|id=ex-q-1>> Since I times omega is fixed, when the moment of inertia shrinks the angular velocity must grow in exactly the same proportion. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I_1\omega_1 = I_2\omega_2|id=eq-4|boxed>> We start by taking both wheels together as one system and writing down the total angular momentum before they couple. The first wheel contributes I times omega, and the second, being at rest, contributes zero. So the initial total angular momentum equals I times omega plus zero, which is I times omega. <<WRITE_STEP:L initial = I omega + 0 = I omega|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now, when the second wheel is dropped on, the two wheels slip and rub against each other, exerting forces of friction. That friction is an internal force of the system. No external torque acts on the two-wheel system, so the total angular momentum stays unchanged. <<WRITE_STEP:Friction is internal; no external torque, so L is conserved.|id=ex-step-1-2>> After coupling, the two wheels share a common angular speed, call it omega prime, and their combined moment of inertia is two times I. So the final angular momentum is two I times omega prime. Setting initial equal to final gives I omega equals two I omega prime. <<WRITE_STEP:I omega = 2 I omega prime|id=ex-step-1-3>> Cancelling I from both sides, we solve for omega prime. And the answer is that the common angular speed is omega over two. <<WRITE_ANSWER:omega prime = omega / 2|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:arms-in>> Watch what happens when she pulls her arms in. Her mass moves close to the axis, so I shrinks. To keep the product I times omega fixed, omega must shoot up. <<TRACE:arms-in>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:spin-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:I down, omega up, L fixed|id=text-1>>That is the whole secret. She spins faster because her own muscles only made an internal pull, and internal forces can never touch the angular momentum.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about angular impulse, which is a beautiful idea that connects torque, time, and angular momentum. You might already remember from straight-line motion that when you apply a force over a span of time, you get something called impulse, and that impulse changes an object's momentum. Angular impulse is the rotating version of exactly the same story.

Here's the setup. Imagine you have a torque acting on a spinning body. Torque, remember, is the twisting effort that tries to change how something rotates. Now, that torque might not stay the same the whole time. It could be strong at first and weaker later, or it could change in any way you like. So to find the total angular impulse, we add up the torque over every tiny instant during the time interval. In the language of calculus, that adding up is an integral. We write it as the integral of the torque with respect to time, taken from the starting time to the ending time. That total is what we call the angular impulse, and we give it the symbol J.

Now comes the key insight. We know that the resultant torque on a body equals the rate of change of its angular momentum. In words, torque tells you how fast the angular momentum is changing at each moment. If you rearrange that idea, you can say that torque multiplied by a tiny bit of time equals a tiny change in angular momentum. So when you add up all those little pieces over the whole interval, the left side becomes the angular impulse, and the right side becomes the total change in angular momentum.

The result is wonderfully simple. The angular impulse of the resultant torque equals the angular momentum at the end minus the angular momentum at the beginning. In other words, the change in angular momentum is equal to the angular impulse.

Why does this matter? Because sometimes you don't care about the messy details of how the torque varied from moment to moment. You just want to know the overall effect on the spinning. Angular impulse lets you skip the complications and connect a twisting effort over time directly to how much the rotation changed. It's the same powerful shortcut that ordinary impulse gives you for straight-line motion, just applied to things that turn.

events.text: Angular impulse = area under the torque-time graph

topics.standalone_narration_text: Give a merry-go-round one hard shove and it spins. Give it a long, gentle push and it ends up spinning just as fast. So a big twist for a short time can match a small twist for a long time. That hints that what really matters is the twist combined with how long it lasts. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:torque-axis>> <<FOCUS:torque-axis>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_11:torque_time_graph>> <<SECTION:Angular Impulse|id=sec-1>>The twisting effort is called torque, and let us put it on a graph against time to see this clearly. Here time runs along the bottom, and torque rises up the side. In real life the torque need not stay steady, so let us draw it strong at first and fading later. <<TRACE:torque-curve>> <<FOCUS:thin-strip>> Now look at one tiny sliver of time, so thin we can treat the torque as constant across it. The little contribution to the spin is just torque times that tiny duration. <<POINT:thin-strip>> How do we account for the whole push, when the torque keeps changing the entire time? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:area-under-curve>> We simply add up every thin strip across the interval. Stack them all together and they fill the whole region under the curve. <<TRACE:area-under-curve>> <<FOCUS:area-under-curve>> <<WRITE_KEY:Angular impulse = area under the torque-time graph|id=key-1>>That shaded area is the angular impulse. It is torque added up over time, and that sum is what governs the spin. <<PAUSE:short>> The angular impulse is the torque added up over every instant of the time interval, which is the area under the torque-time graph. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \Gamma \, dt|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:area-under-curve>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = \int_{t_1}^{t_2} \Gamma \, dt|id=eq-1>>In symbols, the angular impulse J is the integral of the torque Gamma over the time interval. <<FOCUS:thin-strip>> <<SECTION:The Payoff|id=sec-2>>Now here is the beautiful part. Torque is the rate at which angular momentum changes, so torque times a tiny time equals a tiny change in angular momentum. Since torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, adding up torque over time gives the total change in angular momentum, the final value minus the initial value. <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = L_2 - L_1|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<FOCUS:area-under-curve>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:J = L_2 - L_1|id=eq-2>>Add up all those tiny changes, and the total angular impulse is exactly the final angular momentum minus the initial one. So the change in a body's spin is never about torque alone, but always torque multiplied by how long it acts, and that equals the change in angular momentum. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:area-under-curve>> That is why the hard shove and the long gentle push give the same final spin. They sweep out the same area, the same angular impulse, the same change in angular momentum. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about what happens when a solid object spins around an axis. Every tiny piece of that object is moving, so every piece carries kinetic energy. The clever idea here is to add up the kinetic energy of all those pieces and see what we get.

Imagine a rigid body turning about a line with some angular speed, which we call omega. Pick any one particle inside the body. It travels in a circle of some radius, the distance from the axis. Its linear speed is just omega times that radius. Now, the kinetic energy of a single particle is one half its mass times its speed squared. Since its speed is omega times the radius, its kinetic energy becomes one half times the mass times omega squared times the radius squared.

Now here's the beautiful part. To get the energy of the whole body, we add up this expression for every particle. The angular speed omega is the same for every particle, because the whole rigid body turns together. So we can pull omega squared outside the sum. What's left inside is the sum of each mass times its radius squared, and that quantity is exactly what we call the moment of inertia. So the total kinetic energy of a rotating rigid body is one half times the moment of inertia times omega squared.

Notice how nicely this mirrors the ordinary kinetic energy of a moving object, which is one half mass times velocity squared. In the rotational version, the moment of inertia plays the role of mass, and omega plays the role of velocity. That's a pattern you'll see again and again in rotational mechanics.

I want you to hold onto one honest point the book makes. This rotational kinetic energy is not some brand-new kind of energy. It's still just plain old kinetic energy, the one half mass times speed squared of every particle, all added together. We just found a tidy way to write that total using the moment of inertia and the angular speed. So when you use this formula, you're really tracking the same motion energy, only organized in terms of how the body spins rather than how each piece moves separately. That insight lets us solve problems where spinning and sliding happen at the same time using simple energy conservation.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about what happens when a torque acts on a spinning object. You already know that when you push something with a force and it moves, you do work on it, and the rate at which you do that work is called power. Well, rotation works in a very similar way, just with the rotational versions of those quantities.

Imagine a rigid body spinning about a fixed axis, and there's a torque acting on it. That torque produces angular acceleration, which means the object spins faster and faster. As it spins faster, its rotational kinetic energy goes up. Here's the key idea: the rate at which that kinetic energy increases is exactly the rate at which work is being done on the body, and that rate of doing work is what we call power.

So let's build the formula in words. The rotational kinetic energy is one half times the moment of inertia times the angular velocity squared. If we look at how fast this energy changes over time, and we work through it carefully, we find that the power delivered equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration times the angular velocity. But notice that the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration is just the torque. So the power delivered by a torque equals the torque times the angular velocity. That's a beautifully simple result, and I want you to compare it to the straight-line case, where power equals force times velocity. The rotational version just swaps force for torque and velocity for angular velocity.

Now, what about the work itself? Power is the rate of doing work, so if we know the power over a tiny slice of time, we can find the tiny bit of work done. Working through it, the small amount of work done equals the torque times the small angular displacement. Again, compare this to the straight-line case where work is force times displacement. Same pattern.

Finally, if the body rotates through a larger angle, say from one angle to a second angle, the total work done is simply the sum, or integral, of the torque over all those tiny angular displacements. If the torque happens to be constant, that just becomes torque times the total angle turned. So the whole story here is about recognizing that rotation mirrors linear motion, with torque, angular velocity, and angle playing the roles of force, velocity, and distance.
