topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:wheel-body>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_13:spinning_wheel_torque>> When you spin a bike wheel by pushing the pedal harder and harder, you're pouring energy into it every single second — and there's a beautifully simple way to count exactly how fast. Here's our wheel, free to turn about this fixed axis, and a torque is acting on it, twisting it the same way it's already spinning. <<POINT:torque-arrow>> <<FOCUS:omega-arrow>> Because that torque produces angular acceleration, the wheel spins faster and faster, and as it speeds up its rotational kinetic energy keeps climbing. Now think back to straight-line motion: when a force makes something speed up, the rate at which its kinetic energy grows is exactly the power being delivered to it. <<FOCUS:wheel-body>> So here's the honest question — if energy is flowing into this wheel every second, how fast is it actually arriving? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Power from a torque|id=sec-1>>The rate of increase of kinetic energy IS the power, so let's just differentiate the rotational kinetic energy and see what falls out. The rotational kinetic energy is one half I omega squared, and when we ask how fast that changes, the moment of inertia I stays constant and only omega is changing. Differentiating gives I times omega times the rate of change of omega — and that rate of change of omega is just the angular acceleration alpha. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Power delivered: P = Gamma times omega|id=key-1>>But I times alpha is simply the torque Gamma, so the power is torque times angular velocity, P equals Gamma times omega — that's our answer. <<PAUSE:short>> The power is the rate of change of one half I omega squared, which works out to I times omega times alpha, and since I times alpha is the torque, it equals torque times angular velocity. <<WRITE_EQUATION:P = \frac{dK}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}\left(\tfrac{1}{2}I\omega^2\right) = I\omega\alpha = \Gamma\omega|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<FOCUS:omega-arrow>> Look how clean that is: the power delivered by a torque is just the torque multiplied by the angular velocity, the perfect mirror of force times velocity in straight-line motion. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rim-point>> <<SECTION:Work done by a torque|id=sec-2>>Now, power is work done per second, so in a tiny slice of time the little bit of work is power times that time, which is Gamma times omega times d t. But omega times d t is just the small angle the wheel turns through, d theta — so each small bit of work is simply torque times the angle turned. <<TRACE:rim-point>> <<PAUSE:short>> In a tiny turn, the work done is the torque times the small angle the body rotates through. <<WRITE_EQUATION:dW = \Gamma\, d\theta|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:W = \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \Gamma\, d\theta|id=eq-work>>Add up all those slices as the wheel turns from one angle to another, and the total work is the integral of torque with respect to angle. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:torque-arrow>> So remember the pair: power is torque times angular velocity, and work is torque summed over the angle turned — the rotational twins of force times velocity and force times distance. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding:
In this section we learn how to actually calculate the moment of inertia for real objects. Remember, the moment of inertia about a line is found by taking each particle's mass, multiplying it by the square of its perpendicular distance from that line, and adding all those products together. When an object is made of just a few separate masses, you can use this directly — just sum up mass times distance squared for each piece.

But most real objects, like rods, plates, rings, and spheres, are continuous lumps of matter, not a handful of points. For those we use a beautiful trick from calculus called integration. The idea is simple: imagine slicing the object into tiny elements, each so small that every point in it sits at almost exactly the same distance from the axis. For one tiny element of mass we write its little moment of inertia as that distance squared times its mass, then we add up — integrate — all those tiny contributions over the whole body. Choosing the right shape for your tiny element is the real art here. For a rod you slice it into little segments along its length. For a circular plate you slice it into thin rings, like the rings inside a tree trunk. For a solid sphere you peel it into thin hollow shells, like layers of an onion.

Watch how cleverly we reuse earlier results. Once we know the moment of inertia of a thin ring, we can build up a full disc by stacking rings. Once we know a hollow sphere, we can build a solid sphere by stacking shells. This layering approach saves enormous effort.

There's one more lovely insight worth noticing. For the hollow sphere we get the same answer two ways — once by direct integration over angle, and once by a slick argument using the three perpendicular axes. Since the sphere looks the same in every direction, all three axes give the same moment of inertia, and adding them up gives a quick path to the answer. By the end you'll have a whole toolbox of standard formulas: a rod about its center, a plate, a ring, a disc, cylinders, and both hollow and solid spheres. These show up again and again, so it's worth understanding how each one is built, not just memorizing the result.

topics.standalone_narration_text: A solid rod and a ring of exactly the same mass — spin them both, and one fights back far harder than the other. Why? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Where the resistance lives|id=sec-1>>The answer is that what matters isn't just how much mass you have, but where that mass sits relative to the axis you spin around. <<PAUSE:short>> Take each tiny piece of the object, multiply its mass by the square of its distance from the axis, and add every one of those up — that total is the moment of inertia. <<PAUSE:short>> Take each tiny piece, multiply its mass by the square of its distance from the axis, and add them all up. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2|id=eq-1|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:I = \sum_i m_i r_i^2|id=eq-1>>For a handful of separate masses this is easy: just compute mass times distance squared for each one and add them together. Notice that square sitting in the formula — it's why mass placed far out is so punishing. <<PAUSE:short>> Double the distance and that piece contributes four times as much resistance, even though its mass hasn't changed at all. But real objects — rods, plates, rings, spheres — aren't a few dots. They're continuous lumps of matter. So how do we add up infinitely many pieces? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rod-body>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_14:sliced_rod>> Here's the beautiful trick from calculus. We slice the object into elements so tiny that every point in one slice sits at essentially the same distance from the axis. <<TRACE:rod-body>> <<FOCUS:mass-element>> Look at one thin slice of this rod, a distance x from the axis, carrying a tiny mass we call dm. <<POINT:mass-element>> <<FOCUS:distance-x>> <<WRITE_STEP:Contribution of one slice: dI = x squared dm|id=step-1>>That single slice contributes its mass dm times x squared, exactly like one particle in our sum. <<FOCUS:length-label>> <<WRITE_KEY:Sum over particles becomes an integral over the body|id=key-1>>Now add up every slice as it slides from the axis along the whole length — the sum becomes an integral over the entire body. <<PAUSE:short>> Add up every infinitesimal slice's mass times its distance squared, and the sum becomes an integral over the whole body. <<WRITE_EQUATION:I = \int r^2 \, dm|id=eq-2|boxed>> <<WRITE_EQUATION:I = \int r^2 \, dm|id=eq-2>>And that's the master tool: integrate r squared dm across the object, and you can find the moment of inertia of any shape you like. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:axis-line>> So back to our puzzle: the ring keeps all its mass out at the rim, far from the centre, while the rod spreads mass right down to the axis. Same mass, but the ring's r squared is bigger everywhere — so the ring fights back harder. <<PAUSE:short>>

topics.our_understanding:
In this section we learn two clever shortcuts that save us a huge amount of work when calculating moment of inertia. Remember, moment of inertia tells us how hard it is to spin an object, and it depends on where the spin axis is. Calculating it from scratch every time would be exhausting, so these two theorems let us reuse results we already know.

The first one is the parallel axes theorem. Imagine you already know the moment of inertia of a body about a line that passes right through its centre of mass. Now you want the moment of inertia about a different line that is parallel to the first one. The theorem says you just take the moment of inertia about the centre of mass line, and add to it the mass of the body times the square of the distance between the two lines. That extra term, mass times distance squared, is the penalty you pay for moving the axis away from the centre of mass. Notice that this means the moment of inertia is always smallest when the axis goes through the centre of mass. The proof works by writing out the positions of every particle and using the fact that the sum of mass times position, measured from the centre of mass, is zero. That neat cancellation is what makes the theorem so clean.

The second one is the perpendicular axes theorem, and this one only works for flat, plane bodies like a thin ring or a disc. Picture the object lying flat in a plane, with an x-axis and a y-axis drawn in that plane and a z-axis sticking straight up through it. The theorem says the moment of inertia about the z-axis equals the moment of inertia about the x-axis plus the moment of inertia about the y-axis. It falls out simply because the distance of any particle from the z-axis squared is just its x-distance squared plus its y-distance squared.

Finally, we meet the radius of gyration. This is a way of describing how spread out the mass effectively is. We imagine squeezing all the mass onto a single ring whose radius gives the same moment of inertia. That radius is the radius of gyration. For a uniform disc, for example, it turns out to be the radius divided by the square root of two. These three ideas together make moment of inertia problems much friendlier.

book_examples.verbatim_text: Example 10.10. Find the moment of inertia of a uniform ring of mass M and radius R about a diameter. Solution: Let AB and CD be two mutually perpendicular diameters of the ring. Take them as X and Y-axes and the line perpendicular to the plane of the ring through the centre as the Z-axis. The moment of inertia of the ring about the Z-axis is I = MR squared. As the ring is uniform, all of its diameters are equivalent and so Ix = Iy. From perpendicular axes theorem, Iz = Ix + Iy. Hence Ix = Iz over 2 = MR squared over 2. Similarly, the moment of inertia of a uniform disc about a diameter is MR squared over 4.

The moment of inertia of the cylinder about its own axis is M times R squared divided by two. <<WRITE_STEP:I0 = M R^2 / 2|id=ex-step-1-1>> Now we use the parallel axes theorem, which says I equals I-naught plus M times d squared. Since the new axis is parallel and sits on the surface, the shift distance d equals R. <<WRITE_STEP:I = I0 + M d^2,  d = R|id=ex-step-1-2>> Substituting, we get M R squared over two plus M times R squared, which adds up to three halves times M times R squared. <<WRITE_STEP:I = M R^2 / 2 + M R^2 = (3/2) M R^2|id=ex-step-1-3>> The same trick works for a solid sphere. Its moment of inertia about its centre is two fifths M times R squared, so about a tangent it becomes two fifths M R squared plus M R squared, which is seven fifths times M times R squared. <<WRITE_STEP:Sphere: (2/5) M R^2 + M R^2 = (7/5) M R^2|id=ex-step-1-4>> And the answer for the cylinder is three halves times M times R squared. <<WRITE_ANSWER:I = (3/2) M R^2|id=ex-ans-1>> Here's an example from the chapter. Take a uniform disc of radius r, and let's find its radius of gyration about its own axis. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Find the radius of gyration of a uniform disc of radius r about its axis|id=ex-q-1>> The radius of gyration k is defined by the relation I equals M times k squared, so k is the square root of I over M. For a uniform disc about its axis, the moment of inertia I equals one half M r squared. <<WRITE_STEP:I = M k^2  so  k = sqrt(I / M)|id=ex-step-1-1>><<WRITE_STEP:I = (1/2) M r^2|id=ex-step-1-2>> Substituting, k equals the square root of one half M r squared divided by M, which is the square root of r squared over two. So the radius of gyration of a uniform disc of radius r about its axis is r divided by the square root of two. <<WRITE_STEP:k = sqrt((1/2) M r^2 / M) = sqrt(r^2 / 2)|id=ex-step-1-3>><<WRITE_ANSWER:k = r / sqrt(2)|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:centre-of-mass>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Lightest spin axis passes through centre of mass|id=text-1>>The centre of mass is the single easiest place to put the axis. Every parallel line away from it costs you M d squared more. <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> There is a companion shortcut for thin flat plates, the perpendicular axes theorem, that adds the moments about two in-plane axes to get the one sticking straight out, but the parallel axes idea is the workhorse you will reach for again and again.

topics.our_understanding:
Up to now we've talked about two clean types of motion. Pure translation, where every part of an object moves the same way in a straight line, like a box sliding across a floor. And pure rotation, where the object spins about a fixed axle. But most real motion is a mix of both. Think of a wheel rolling down a road. It spins, and at the same time its center moves forward. That's combined rotation and translation, and that's what this section is about.

The clever idea here is to split the messy motion into two simpler pieces. Imagine watching the body from a special frame of reference that rides along with it. In that moving frame, the body looks like it's just spinning. Then, to get the full picture as seen from the ground, you add the motion of that frame back in. So the total motion equals the spinning part plus the moving-along part.

Now here's the tricky bit. The frame riding along with the body is usually accelerating, which makes it noninertial. In a noninertial frame, our familiar rule that torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration normally fails, because we'd have to add pretend forces, called pseudo forces, to every particle. Those pseudo forces could create a pseudo torque and ruin the equation.

But there's a beautiful escape. If you choose your axis to pass through the center of mass, all those pseudo torques add up to exactly zero. Why? Because when you measure positions from the center of mass, the sum of mass times position is zero, by the very definition of the center of mass. So the pseudo torque vanishes, and the equation torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration survives, as long as everything is measured about the center of mass.

This gives us a wonderfully simple working rule. First, list all the external forces. Add them up as vectors and divide by the total mass. That gives you the acceleration of the center of mass. Second, find the total external torque about a line through the center of mass, perpendicular to the plane of motion, and find the moment of inertia about that same line. Divide torque by moment of inertia, and you get the angular acceleration about the center of mass. Notice this line might not even be the real axis of rotation seen from the ground, but you still calculate everything about it. With these two results, plus the starting conditions, you can completely predict how the body will move.

10.17 ROLLING
When you go on a bicycle on a straight road what
distance on the road is covered during one full pedal ?
Suppose a particular spoke of the bicycle is painted
black and is vertical at some instant pointing
downward. After one full pedal the spoke is again
vertical in the similar position. We say that the wheel
has made one full rotation. During this period the
bicycle has moved through a distance 2πR in normal
180
Concepts of Physics

cycling on a good, free road. Here R is the radius of
the wheel. The wheels are said to be ‘rolling’ on the
road.
Looking from the road frame, the wheel is not
making pure rotation about a fixed line. The particles
of the wheel do not go on circles. The path of a particle
at the rim will be something like that shown in figure
(10.27), whereas the centre of the wheel goes in a
straight line. But we still say that during one pedal
the wheel has made one rotation, i.e., it has rotated
through an angle of 2. By this we mean that the spoke
that was vertical (pointing downward from the centre)
again became vertical in the similar position. In this
period the centre of the wheel has moved through a
distance 2R. In half of this period, the wheel has
moved through a distance  R and the spoke makes
an angle of  with its original direction. During a short
time-interval t, the wheel moves through a distance
x and the spoke rotates by . Thus the wheel rotates
and at the same time moves forward. The relation
between the displacement of (the centre of) the wheel
and the angle rotated by (a spoke of) the wheel is
x  R. Dividing by t and taking limits, we get
            v  R,
where v is the linear speed of the centre of mass and
 is the angular velocity of the wheel.
This type of motion of a wheel (or any other object
with circular boundary) in which the centre of the
wheel moves in a straight line and the wheel rotates
in its plane about its centre with v  R, is called pure
rolling.
Place a ring on a horizontal surface as shown in
figure (10.28) and put your finger on the lowest part.
Use other hand to rotate the ring a little while the
finger 
is 
kept 
on 
the 
lowest 
point. 
This 
is
approximately a small part of rolling motion. Note the
displacements of different particles of the ring. The
centre has moved forward a little, say x. The topmost
point has moved approximately double of this distance.
The part in contact with the horizontal surface below
the finger has almost been in the same position.
In pure rolling, the velocity of the contact point is
zero. The velocity of the centre of mass is vcm  R and
that of the topmost point is vtop  2R  2vcm.
Next, consider another type of combination of
rotation and translation, in which the wheel moves
through a distance greater than 2R in one full
rotation. Hold the ring of figure (10.28) between three
fingers, apply a forward force to move it fast on the
table and rotate it slowly through the fingers. Its
angular velocity   d/dt is small and vcm  R. This
is a case of rolling with forward slipping. This type of
motion occurs when you apply sudden brakes to the
bicycle on a road which is fairly smooth after rain. The
cycle stops after a long distance and the wheel rotates
only little during this period. If you look at the
particles in contact, these will be found rubbing the
road in the forward direction. The particles in contact
have a velocity in the forward direction. In this case
vcm > R. An extreme example of this type occurs
when the wheel does not rotate at all and translates
with linear velocity v. Then vcm  v  and    0.
Yet another type of rolling with slipping occurs
when the wheel moves a distance shorter than 2R
while making one rotation. In this case, the velocity
vcm < R. Hold the ring of figure (10.28) between three
fingers, rotate it fast and translate it slowly. It will
move a small distance on the table and rotate fast. If
you drive a bicycle on a road on which a lot of mud is
present, sometimes the wheel rotates fast but moves
a little. If you look at the particles in contact, they rub
the road in the backward direction. The centre moves
less than 2R during one full rotation and vcm < R.
These situations may be visualised in a different
manner which gives another interpretation of rolling.
Consider a wheel of radius r with its axis fixed in a
second-hand car. The wheel may rotate freely about
this axis. Suppose the floor of the second-hand car has
a hole in it and the wheel just touches the road through

rotates the wheel at a uniform angular velocity  and
the driver drives the car at a uniform velocity v on the
road which is parallel to the plane of the wheel as
shown in figure (10.29). The two motions are
independent. The backseater is rotating the wheel at
an angular velocity according to his will and the driver
is driving the car at a velocity according to his will.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about what happens when you ride a bicycle on a straight road. Imagine you paint one spoke of the wheel black, and right now it points straight down. After one full pedal, that spoke comes back to the same downward position. We say the wheel has made one full rotation. During that one rotation, how far did you travel? On a good road, you moved forward a distance equal to two times pi times the radius of the wheel. That's exactly the circumference, the distance around the rim. The wheel is rolling.

Now here's the interesting part. If you watch the wheel from the side of the road, it isn't doing pure spinning around a fixed line, and it isn't doing pure straight-line motion either. It's doing both at once. The centre of the wheel travels in a straight line, while the wheel spins around that centre. A point on the rim traces out a looping, curvy path. So during a tiny time interval, the centre moves forward a small distance, and the spoke rotates by a small angle. The relationship between these is beautiful and simple: the forward distance equals the radius times the angle turned. If you divide by time and look at how fast things happen, you get the key rule of pure rolling: the speed of the centre equals the radius times the angular velocity.

Now here's something that surprises many students. In pure rolling, the point at the very bottom, the one touching the ground, is momentarily not moving at all. Its velocity is zero. Meanwhile, the centre moves at speed v, and the topmost point actually moves at double that, twice v. Try it with a ring on a table to see this for yourself.

But rolling isn't always perfect. If you slam the brakes on a wet road, the wheel slides forward while barely spinning. Then the centre moves faster than radius times angular velocity, and we call it rolling with forward slipping. The contact point rubs the road forward. The extreme case is a wheel that doesn't spin at all but slides. The opposite happens in mud: the wheel spins fast but moves little, so the centre moves slower than radius times angular velocity. That's backward slipping, where the contact point rubs the road backward. A clever way to see all this is to picture the wheel's spin and the car's forward motion as two separate choices, and the contact point's true velocity is the sum of both.

So the answer is: this is rolling with backward slipping. <<WRITE_ANSWER:velocity of contact with respect to road = minus omega r plus v, which is less than zero, so this is rolling with backward slipping|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:centre-point>> <<WRITE_STEP:speed of centre = R times spin rate|id=step-1>>Divide both by the time taken, and you get a beautifully simple link: the speed of the centre equals the radius times how fast the wheel spins. <<POINT:centre-point>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:wheel-circle>> So a rolling wheel is never just spinning and never just sliding. topics.our_understanding:
Imagine a wheel rolling down a road. It's doing two things at once. It's spinning around its own center, and that whole center is also gliding forward across the ground. So when we ask how much kinetic energy this rolling body has, we need to account for both kinds of motion together. That's exactly what this section figures out.

Here's the beautiful result the textbook works toward. The total kinetic energy of a body that is both rotating and translating splits cleanly into two separate pieces that simply add together. The first piece is the energy of rotation about the center of mass, which is one half times the moment of inertia about the center of mass times the angular velocity squared. The second piece is the energy of the whole body moving along, which is one half times the total mass times the speed of the center of mass squared. Add those two and you have the complete kinetic energy.

Why does it split so neatly? When you write each particle's speed as its speed in the center-of-mass frame plus the speed of the center of mass itself, and you square that and sum it all up, a cross term appears in the middle. But that cross term involves the velocity of the center of mass measured in the center-of-mass frame, and in that frame the center of mass isn't moving at all, so the term is zero. That's the magic. The two energies don't get tangled up; they stay separate.

Now think about pure rolling, where there's no slipping. In that case the forward speed of the center equals the radius times the angular velocity. When you plug that relationship in, the two energy terms combine into one tidy expression. And using the parallel axis theorem, that combined moment of inertia is exactly the moment of inertia about the line touching the ground at the point of contact. So the kinetic energy becomes simply one half times that moment of inertia times the angular velocity squared.

That gives us a lovely new way to picture rolling. At any instant, a rolling body behaves as if it's purely rotating about the point where it touches the ground. That contact point acts like a momentary pivot, and the pivot itself slides forward as the body rolls along. Both viewpoints, rotation-plus-translation or pure rotation about the contact point, give the same energy. It's the same physics seen two ways.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's think about a body that's doing two things at once: it's spinning, and it's also moving through space. A rolling wheel is the perfect picture. The wheel spins around its own center, and at the same time the whole wheel travels down the road. We want to figure out the total angular momentum of such a body about some fixed point in the lab, which we'll call O.

Here's the clever trick. The position of any little piece of the body can be split into two parts: where that piece sits relative to the center of mass, plus where the center of mass sits relative to O. In the same way, the velocity of any piece is its velocity relative to the center of mass, plus the velocity of the center of mass itself. So we describe each tiny piece using these two ingredients.

When you plug these split-up positions and velocities into the formula for angular momentum and carefully multiply everything out, you get four terms. Now, two of those four terms quietly vanish, and that's the beautiful part. They vanish because of what the center of mass actually means. By definition, the sum of mass times position measured from the center of mass is zero, and the sum of mass times velocity measured from the center of mass is also zero. The center of mass is the balance point, so these add up to nothing.

What survives is just two terms. The first term is the angular momentum of the body as seen by someone riding along with the center of mass, watching only the spinning. We call this the angular momentum about the center of mass. The second term treats the entire mass of the body as if it were squished into a single point at the center of mass, moving with the center-of-mass velocity, and asks for the angular momentum of that single moving point about O.

So here's the key insight to carry away: the total angular momentum of a body that's both spinning and traveling is simply the spin part plus the travel part. The spinning contribution, measured about its own center, plus the contribution of the whole mass moving as one lump. This neat separation makes complicated rolling and tumbling problems far easier, because you can handle the spin and the motion of the center separately and then just add them together.

10.20 WHY DOES A ROLLING SPHERE
     SLOW DOWN ?
When a sphere is rolled on a horizontal table it
slows down and eventually stops. Figure (10.30) shows
the situation. The forces acting on the sphere are (a)
weight mg, (b) friction at the contact and (c) the normal
force. As the centre of the sphere decelerates, the
friction should be opposite to its velocity, that is
towards left in figure (10.30). But this friction will have
a clockwise torque that should increase the angular
velocity of the sphere. There must be an anticlockwise
torque that causes the decrease in the angular velocity.
In fact, when the sphere rolls on the table, both
the sphere and the surface deform near the contact.
The contact is not at a single point as we normally

topics.our_understanding: Here's a puzzle that sounds simple but hides something subtle. When you roll a sphere across a table, it slows down and eventually stops. The question is, why? Let's think carefully. There are three forces acting on the sphere. There's its weight pulling straight down, there's the normal force from the table pushing up, and there's friction at the point of contact. Now, as the center of the sphere slows down, friction must point backward, opposite to the direction the sphere is moving. So far so good. But here's the trick. That backward friction, acting at the bottom of the sphere, creates a twisting effect, a torque, that would actually spin the sphere faster, not slower. Picture it. If friction pushes back at the bottom, it tends to make the ball roll more, increasing its spinning. So friction alone cannot explain why the spinning slows down. There must be some other twist working in the opposite direction, an anticlockwise torque, that brings the rotation to a halt. So where does it come from? The answer is that the real world is not as clean as our idealized pictures. We usually imagine the sphere touching the table at a single perfect point. But in reality, both the sphere and the table squash a little near the contact. Instead of a single point, there's a small area of contact. And here's the key insight. The front part of that contact area presses against the table a bit more strongly than the back part. Because of this uneven pressing, the normal force, which we drew straight up through the center, actually gets shifted forward, toward the front of the sphere. Once the normal force no longer passes through the center, it produces a torque of its own, and that torque is anticlockwise, exactly the kind needed to slow the spinning down. So the full story is that friction slows the forward motion of the center, while the shifted normal force slows the rotation. Together they bring the rolling sphere to rest. The big lesson here is that our neat assumption of a single contact point is just an approximation. When you look closely, surfaces deform, contact spreads out, and tiny shifts in where forces act can explain things that otherwise seem impossible. This is called rolling friction, and it's why nothing rolls forever.

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:sphere>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:rotational_mechanics:10_20:rolling_sphere_forces>> Roll a ball across a table and it always slows down and stops. Simple, right? But there's a hidden trap here that fools almost everyone. <<SECTION:The three forces|id=sec-1>>Let's be careful and draw every force on the ball. First, its weight pulls straight down through the centre. <<POINT:weight-arrow>> Second, the table pushes back up with the normal force. And third, there's friction right at the point where the ball touches the table. <<POINT:normal-arrow>> <<FOCUS:friction-arrow>> Now the ball is moving to the right and slowing down, so friction must point backward, to the left, opposing the motion. That feels completely natural. <<POINT:friction-arrow>> <<FOCUS:friction-arrow>> But watch what that backward friction does to the spinning. It pushes left at the very bottom of the ball. Here's the puzzle: a backward shove at the bottom is exactly what makes a ball roll faster, not slower. That friction gives a clockwise torque that should speed the spin up. So why doesn't the ball spin faster forever? <<TRACE:friction-arrow>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:sphere>> <<WRITE_KEY:Friction speeds the spin up, so it can't be what stops the sphere|id=key-1>>So friction can't be the villain. If anything, it would keep the ball rolling. We need another torque, a braking one, that we haven't drawn yet. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:contact-area>> <<SECTION:The contact is not a point|id=sec-2>>The trick is an assumption we made without noticing. We drew the ball touching the table at a single point. In reality, both the ball and the table squash a little, and they touch over a small area. <<TRACE:contact-area>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:normal-shift>> And here's the payoff: as the ball rolls forward, its front edge presses into the table harder than its trailing edge. So the upward push isn't centred underneath, it bunches up toward the front. <<POINT:normal-shift>> <<FOCUS:normal-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Normal force shifts forward, off the centre line|id=text-1>>That means the normal force no longer points straight up through the centre. It's shifted forward, to the right of the centre. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:normal-shift>> An upward force in front of the centre twists the ball the other way, an anticlockwise torque. That is the genuine brake on the spinning. <<TRACE:normal-shift>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<CLEAR_ANNOTATIONS>> <<FOCUS:sphere>> So the real answer is delightfully sneaky. A rolling sphere slows down because it deforms the surface, the normal force shifts forward, and that off-centre push creates the torque that quietly steals its spin away.
