questions.q_text: During the rotation of a rigid body about a fixed axis, what happens to the particles that lie exactly on the axis of rotation?
options: A. They move in the largest circles
B. They stay still and do not move
C. They move in small circles
D. They move faster than all other particles

questions.q_text: Consider two particles in a rotating rigid body — one close to the axis and one far from it. Which statement is correct about the time each takes to complete one full circle?
options: A. The particle far from the axis takes longer
B. The particle close to the axis takes longer
C. Both take exactly the same time
D. It depends on the mass of each particle

questions.q_text: A fly sits near the edge of a spinning record on a turntable and traces a circle. What does this example demonstrate about the axis of rotation?
options: A. The axis must pass through the heaviest part of the body
B. The axis can lie completely outside the rotating body
C. The axis always passes through the center of the body
D. The fly is not actually rotating

questions.q_text: A ceiling fan rotates about a vertical line through its center. Explain how you would find the center of the circular path traced by a point located at the tip of one of the fan's blades.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the axis of rotation — for the ceiling fan it is the vertical line passing through the fan's center. Step 2: Take the point at the blade tip whose circular path you want to find. Step 3: Drop a straight perpendicular from that tip point down to the axis of rotation. Step 4: The point where this perpendicular meets the axis (the foot of the perpendicular) is the center of the circle that the blade tip traces. Step 5: The distance from the blade tip to this foot is the radius of its circular path; since the tip is far from the axis, this circle is large.

questions.q_text: On a spinning turntable, particle A sits 2 centimeters from the central axis and particle B sits 8 centimeters from the same axis. Compare the sizes of their circular paths and the time each takes to complete one full loop. Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: Step 1: The size of a particle's circle depends on its distance from the axis. Particle B is 8 cm from the axis while particle A is only 2 cm away, so particle B's circle has a larger radius — in fact 4 times larger — and therefore a larger circumference. Step 2: This means particle B travels a greater distance in one loop than particle A. Step 3: However, in a rigid body all particles turn together as one, so every particle completes one full loop in exactly the same amount of time. Step 4: Therefore particle B traces a bigger circle than particle A, but both take the same time per loop. (Since B covers a longer path in the same time, it must move faster, but the time per revolution is identical.)

questions.q_text: For a rigid body spinning about a fixed axis, which quantity is the same for every particle in the body at any given moment?
options: A. The linear speed
B. The angular position theta
C. The tangential acceleration
D. The distance travelled along its circle

questions.q_text: Two particles in a spinning rigid body are at different distances from the axis, one near the centre and one near the edge. Which statement is correct?
options: A. Both have the same linear speed but different angular speeds
B. The particle near the edge has greater linear speed but the same angular speed
C. The particle near the centre has greater linear speed
D. Both have the same linear speed and the same angular speed

questions.q_text: A ceiling fan starts from rest and reaches an angular speed of 12 radians per second in 4 seconds with constant angular acceleration. Find its angular acceleration and the angle it turns through in those 4 seconds.
questions.answer: Start with omega equals omega-naught plus alpha times t. Here omega-naught is 0 (starts from rest), omega is 12 radians per second, and t is 4 seconds. So 12 equals 0 plus alpha times 4, giving alpha equals 12 divided by 4, which is 3 radians per second squared. For the angle, use theta equals omega-naught times t plus one half alpha t squared. With omega-naught equal to 0: theta equals one half times 3 times 4 squared, which is one half times 3 times 16, equal to 24 radians. So the angular acceleration is 3 radians per second squared and the fan turns through 24 radians.

questions.q_text: A point on a rotating disc is 0.5 metres from the axis. The disc spins at a constant angular speed of 10 radians per second. What is the linear speed of that point, and what is its tangential acceleration?
questions.answer: Linear speed along the tangent is v equals r times omega. With r equal to 0.5 metres and omega equal to 10 radians per second, v equals 0.5 times 10, which is 5 metres per second. The tangential acceleration is r times alpha. Since the angular speed is constant, alpha equals 0, so the tangential acceleration is 0.5 times 0, which is 0. So the point moves at 5 metres per second with zero tangential acceleration.

questions.q_text: A fan is spinning at 20 radians per second when it is switched off. It decelerates uniformly and stops after turning through 100 radians. Find the angular deceleration.
questions.answer: Use omega squared equals omega-naught squared plus two alpha theta. The final angular speed omega is 0, omega-naught is 20 radians per second, and theta is 100 radians. So 0 equals 20 squared plus 2 times alpha times 100. That is 0 equals 400 plus 200 times alpha. Solving, 200 times alpha equals minus 400, so alpha equals minus 2 radians per second squared. The negative sign shows deceleration, so the angular deceleration is 2 radians per second squared.

questions.q_text: When you switch on a ceiling fan, the blades speed up but the center of the fan stays put. What does the center staying at rest tell us about the external forces on the fan?
options: A. The external forces add up to a large value
B. The external forces all add up to zero
C. There are no external forces acting at all
D. The external forces point only downward

questions.q_text: The section presents two facts that seem to contradict each other. Which pair correctly states them?
options: A. Angular acceleration always requires net force, and net force always produces spinning
B. You can have angular acceleration with zero net force, yet you cannot get angular acceleration with no external force at all
C. The center of mass always moves when something spins, and net force is always zero
D. Torque equals force, and force equals angular acceleration

questions.q_text: Why does the section conclude that plain net force is not the right quantity to decide whether something starts to spin?
options: A. Because force is too hard to measure
B. Because a fan with zero net force still speeds up its spin, so net force can't be what causes the spinning
C. Because force only acts in straight lines and fans are round
D. Because the fan's center of mass moves when it spins

questions.q_text: According to the section, what is torque best described as?
options: A. The same thing as the net force on an object
B. The rotational cousin of force, the quantity that actually produces angular acceleration
C. The speed at which the blades spin
D. The position of the center of mass

questions.q_text: Explain, step by step, why the ceiling fan example forces us to introduce a new quantity (torque) instead of relying on net force alone.
questions.answer: Step 1: Observe the fan. When switched on, its blades spin faster and faster — this speeding up of the spin is angular acceleration. Step 2: Notice the center of mass of the fan does not move; it stays mounted in place. Step 3: When the center of mass stays at rest, the total external force on the object must be zero (the forces cancel). Step 4: So we have a case where there is angular acceleration AND the net force is zero at the same time. Step 5: If net force were what causes spinning, then a zero net force could never produce angular acceleration — but it clearly does here. This contradiction shows net force is not the correct quantity for rotation. Step 6: At the same time, we know that without any external force you cannot start something spinning (a wheel won't turn by itself; you must push it). So something must act — but it isn't simply the sum of forces. Step 7: The missing idea must account not only for how hard you push, but where and in what direction relative to the axis. That quantity is torque, the rotational analogue of force, and it is what truly produces angular acceleration.

questions.q_text: A force is applied parallel to the axis of rotation of a rigid body. What is its torque about that axis?
options: A. Equal to the force times the lever arm
B. Zero
C. Maximum, since it acts along the axis
D. Equal to the moment of inertia times angular acceleration

questions.q_text: Why are door handles placed far from the hinges rather than near them?
options: A. To reduce the moment of inertia of the door
B. Because forces near the hinges point along the axis
C. Because a larger lever arm gives a larger torque for the same force
D. Because torque depends on the choice of origin

questions.q_text: When computing the torque of a force about a fixed line, where may you place the origin without changing the result?
options: A. Anywhere in space
B. Anywhere on the line (axis)
C. Only at the point where the force is applied
D. Only at the center of mass of the body

questions.q_text: Two equal and opposite forces act on a rigid body at different points. The net force is zero. What can be said about the net torque?
options: A. It must also be zero, since the forces cancel
B. It can be nonzero, because the forces can still produce a turning effect
C. It equals the force times the distance between the points only if the body is at rest
D. It cannot be determined without knowing the mass

questions.q_text: A mechanic applies a force of 50 newtons perpendicular to the axis of a bolt, along a wrench. The line of action of this force does not intersect the bolt's axis, and the common perpendicular between the force's line and the axis is 0.30 meters. Find the magnitude of the torque about the bolt's axis.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the special case. The force is perpendicular to the axis and does not intersect it, so the torque equals the force times the lever arm (the length of the common perpendicular). Step 2: Identify the values. Force F = 50 newtons, lever arm = 0.30 meters. Step 3: Multiply. Torque = 50 times 0.30 = 15. Step 4: State the result with units. The torque magnitude is 15 newton-meters.

questions.q_text: In rotational motion, the relation 'net external torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration' is analogous to which equation for straight-line motion?
options: A. Force equals mass times velocity
B. Force equals mass times acceleration
C. Work equals force times distance
D. Momentum equals mass times velocity

questions.q_text: For a rigid body to be in complete equilibrium, which two conditions must both be satisfied?
options: A. Zero total force and zero total velocity
B. Zero total force and zero total torque
C. Zero total torque and constant mass
D. Zero acceleration and maximum kinetic energy

questions.q_text: When all forces lie in one plane and the total force is already zero, what is special about the total torque?
options: A. It depends strongly on which reference point you choose
B. It is the same about every perpendicular axis, so if zero about one point it is zero about all
C. It must be computed only about the center of mass
D. It can only be zero if the body is also moving at constant speed

questions.q_text: In stable equilibrium, what happens to the center of mass when the object is given a small displacement?
options: A. It drops to a lower height
B. It stays at the same height
C. It rises to a higher height
D. It moves outside the base

questions.q_text: Why does a person lean away from a heavy bag they are carrying in one hand?
options: A. To increase the weight they can lift
B. To shift their center of mass back over their feet so the vertical line through it stays inside the base
C. To reduce the torque produced by gravity to zero everywhere
D. To make the bag feel lighter by changing its mass

questions.q_text: A light, rigid uniform plank is balanced on a pivot. A child weighing 300 newtons sits 2 meters to the left of the pivot. At what distance from the pivot, on the right side, must a 400 newton adult sit so the plank is in rotational equilibrium?
questions.answer: For rotational equilibrium, the total torque about the pivot must be zero. We choose the pivot as our reference point, which is convenient because the pivot's support force passes through it and produces no torque. The child produces a torque trying to rotate the plank one way: 300 newtons times 2 meters equals 600 newton-meters. For balance, the adult must produce an equal and opposite torque on the other side: 400 newtons times the distance equals 600 newton-meters. Solving for the distance: distance equals 600 divided by 400, which equals 1.5 meters. So the adult must sit 1.5 meters from the pivot on the right side.

questions.q_text: Why must a cyclist lean inward when going around a flat circular curve?
options: A. To balance the torques of weight and centrifugal force so the bike does not topple
B. To reduce the friction between the tire and the road
C. To increase the normal force from the ground
D. To make the centrifugal force disappear completely

questions.q_text: A heavy rider and a light rider take the same curve at the same speed. How do their lean angles compare?
options: A. The heavy rider leans more
B. The light rider leans more
C. They lean by exactly the same angle
D. It depends on the radius only for the heavy rider

questions.q_text: Why are torques taken about the contact point where the wheel meets the road?
options: A. Because the weight acts at that point
B. Because the normal force and friction pass through it, making their torques zero
C. Because the centrifugal force acts at that point
D. Because it is the center of the circular path

questions.q_text: According to the lean formula, what happens to the required lean angle if the cyclist rides faster on the same curve?
options: A. The lean angle decreases
B. The lean angle stays the same
C. The lean angle increases
D. The lean angle becomes zero

questions.q_text: A cyclist rides at 10 meters per second around a flat circular track of radius 50 meters. Taking g as 10 meters per second squared, find the tangent of the angle by which the cyclist must lean.
questions.answer: The lean condition is: tangent of the angle equals speed squared divided by (radius times g). Step 1: speed squared is 10 times 10, which equals 100. Step 2: radius times g is 50 times 10, which equals 500. Step 3: divide: 100 divided by 500 equals 0.2. So the tangent of the lean angle is 0.2. (This corresponds to an angle of about 11.3 degrees.) Notice the mass of the cyclist never entered the calculation, since it cancels out.

questions.q_text: Angular momentum of a particle about a point O is defined as which of the following?
options: A. The dot product of position vector r and momentum p
B. The cross product of position vector r and momentum p
C. Mass times velocity
D. The cross product of velocity and acceleration

questions.q_text: Which statement about the direction of a particle's angular momentum about a point is correct?
options: A. It points along the position vector r
B. It points along the velocity vector
C. It is perpendicular to both r and p
D. It always points vertically upward

questions.q_text: A particle moves in a straight line at constant speed. As the line of its motion is moved farther from the point O (while speed and mass stay the same), what happens to the magnitude of its angular momentum about O?
options: A. It decreases
B. It stays the same
C. It increases
D. It becomes zero

questions.q_text: A particle of mass 2 kilograms moves with a speed of 5 metres per second along a straight line. The perpendicular distance from a point O to this line is 3 metres. Find the magnitude of the particle's angular momentum about O.
questions.answer: The magnitude of angular momentum equals mass times velocity times the perpendicular distance from O to the line of motion. Step 1: identify the values — mass is 2 kilograms, velocity is 5 metres per second, perpendicular distance is 3 metres. Step 2: multiply them together: 2 times 5 times 3. Step 3: 2 times 5 is 10, and 10 times 3 is 30. So the angular momentum about O is 30 kilogram metre squared per second.

questions.q_text: A particle of mass 4 kilograms moves at 3 metres per second. Its position vector from point O has length 2 metres, and the angle between the position vector and the velocity is 30 degrees. Find the magnitude of its angular momentum about O.
questions.answer: The magnitude of angular momentum equals mass times velocity times r times the sine of the angle between r and v. Step 1: write down the values — mass is 4 kilograms, velocity is 3 metres per second, r is 2 metres, and the angle is 30 degrees. Step 2: the sine of 30 degrees is 0.5. Step 3: multiply everything: 4 times 3 times 2 times 0.5. Step 4: 4 times 3 is 12, 12 times 2 is 24, and 24 times 0.5 is 12. So the magnitude of the angular momentum about O is 12 kilogram metre squared per second.

questions.q_text: When we compute the angular momentum of a particle about a line AB by choosing a point O on the line, why does the choice of which point on AB we pick not matter?
options: A. Because the cross product is always zero on a line
B. Because we only take the component of r cross p along the line, and that component comes out the same for any point chosen on the line
C. Because angular momentum does not depend on position at all
D. Because the velocity is always parallel to the line

questions.q_text: In the equation that says angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular velocity, which quantity plays the role that mass plays in linear momentum?
options: A. Angular velocity
B. Moment of inertia
C. Radius
D. Linear velocity

questions.q_text: For a single particle moving in a circle, why does its angular momentum about the center simplify to mass times velocity times radius?
options: A. Because the position and velocity vectors are perpendicular to each other
B. Because the particle moves in a straight line
C. Because the radius equals the velocity
D. Because the mass cancels out in the cross product

questions.q_text: In a rigid body spinning with a single shared angular velocity, how does the linear speed of a particle depend on its distance from the axis?
options: A. Speed is the same for all particles regardless of distance
B. Speed is smaller for particles farther from the axis
C. Speed is larger for particles farther from the axis
D. Speed does not depend on distance, only on mass

questions.q_text: A disc has a moment of inertia of 2 kilogram metres squared about its central axis and spins at an angular velocity of 5 radians per second. Find its angular momentum about that axis.
questions.answer: We use the relationship angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular velocity. Here the moment of inertia is 2 kilogram metres squared and the angular velocity is 5 radians per second. Multiplying these together: 2 times 5 equals 10. So the angular momentum is 10 kilogram metres squared per second, directed along the spin axis.

questions.q_text: Explain step by step why the angular momentum of a whole rigid body spinning about an axis comes out to be its moment of inertia times its angular velocity.
questions.answer: Step 1: Picture the body as many tiny particles, all rotating together about one axis with the same shared angular velocity, call it omega. Step 2: Take one particle, the i-th, going around a circle of radius r-i. Its linear speed is r-i times omega, since speed equals radius times angular velocity. Step 3: For this single particle, angular momentum is mass times velocity times radius, which is mass times (r-i times omega) times r-i, equalling mass times r-i squared times omega. Step 4: To get the total angular momentum, add up these contributions over all particles. Since omega is the same for every particle, we factor it out front, leaving the sum of each mass times its radius squared. Step 5: But that remaining sum — each mass times its distance squared from the axis, added over all particles — is exactly the definition of the moment of inertia of the body about that axis. Step 6: Therefore the total angular momentum equals moment of inertia times omega.

questions.q_text: When we derive that the rate of change of a system's angular momentum equals only the external torque, what happens to the internal torques between particles?
options: A. They add up to give the dominant contribution
B. They cancel out completely in pairs
C. They equal the external torque
D. They cause the angular momentum to slowly decay

questions.q_text: If the total external torque acting on a system is zero, what can we say about its angular momentum?
options: A. It increases steadily
B. It decreases to zero
C. It stays constant
D. It oscillates back and forth

questions.q_text: A spinning ice skater pulls her arms in toward her body. With no external torque acting, what happens to her rotation?
options: A. She spins faster because her moment of inertia decreases
B. She spins slower because her moment of inertia decreases
C. She spins faster because her angular momentum increases
D. Her spin rate stays exactly the same

questions.q_text: A skater spins at 2 revolutions per second with her arms extended, giving her a moment of inertia of 6 kilogram metre squared. She pulls her arms in, reducing her moment of inertia to 2 kilogram metre squared. Assuming no external torque, find her new spin rate.
questions.answer: Since there is no external torque, angular momentum is conserved. Angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular velocity, so the product stays constant. Initial value: 6 times 2 equals 12 (in units of kilogram metre squared times revolutions per second). Final value must also equal 12, so 2 times the new spin rate equals 12. Therefore the new spin rate equals 12 divided by 2, which is 6 revolutions per second. She spins three times faster because her moment of inertia dropped to one third of its original value.

questions.q_text: For a rigid body spinning about a fixed axis whose moment of inertia stays the same, which statement correctly relates the external torque to the motion?
options: A. The external torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular velocity
B. The external torque equals the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration
C. The external torque equals zero whenever the body spins
D. The external torque equals the angular momentum divided by time always

questions.q_text: Why is the conservation of angular momentum so useful for solving rotational problems?
options: A. It lets you ignore the angular velocity entirely
B. It guarantees no torque ever acts on a real system
C. It lets you relate initial and final states without tracking the messy details in between
D. It proves the moment of inertia can never change

questions.q_text: Angular impulse is best defined as which of the following?
options: A. The torque divided by the time interval
B. The integral of torque with respect to time over the interval
C. The angular momentum divided by time
D. The product of moment of inertia and angular velocity

questions.q_text: The angular impulse of the resultant torque on a body is equal to which quantity?
options: A. The final angular momentum only
B. The average torque on the body
C. The change in the body's angular momentum
D. The total kinetic energy gained

questions.q_text: Why is the angular impulse idea especially useful in practice?
options: A. It lets you find the overall change in rotation without tracking how the torque varied moment to moment
B. It removes the need to know the time interval involved
C. It works only when torque is constant the whole time
D. It converts rotational motion into straight-line motion

questions.q_text: A wheel experiences a constant torque of 4 newton-metres for 3 seconds. If its angular momentum at the start was 2 kilogram-metre-squared-per-second, what is its angular momentum at the end?
questions.answer: Step 1: Find the angular impulse. Since the torque is constant, the integral of torque over time is simply torque multiplied by the time interval. So angular impulse equals 4 newton-metres times 3 seconds, which is 12 units of angular momentum. Step 2: Use the principle that the change in angular momentum equals the angular impulse. So the final angular momentum equals the initial angular momentum plus the angular impulse: 2 plus 12 equals 14. Step 3: The final angular momentum is 14 kilogram-metre-squared-per-second.

questions.q_text: A spinning disc's angular momentum increases from 5 to 11 kilogram-metre-squared-per-second over a time interval of 2 seconds. Assuming the torque was constant, what was its value?
questions.answer: Step 1: Find the change in angular momentum, which equals the angular impulse. The change is final minus initial, so 11 minus 5 equals 6 units. Step 2: For a constant torque, the angular impulse equals torque multiplied by the time interval. So 6 equals torque times 2 seconds. Step 3: Solve for torque: torque equals 6 divided by 2, which is 3 newton-metres.

questions.q_text: In the formula for the kinetic energy of a rotating rigid body, which quantity plays the same role that mass plays in ordinary kinetic energy?
options: A. The angular speed omega
B. The moment of inertia
C. The radius of the body
D. The linear velocity

questions.q_text: When we add up the kinetic energy of every particle in a spinning rigid body, why can we pull omega squared outside the sum?
options: A. Because every particle has the same mass
B. Because every particle is the same distance from the axis
C. Because every particle shares the same angular speed in a rigid body
D. Because omega is always equal to one

questions.q_text: According to the honest point the book stresses, what is rotational kinetic energy really?
options: A. A brand-new form of energy unique to spinning objects
B. Just the ordinary kinetic energy of all the particles added together, rewritten
C. A type of potential energy stored in the rotation
D. Energy that exists only when an object also slides

questions.q_text: A solid disc has a moment of inertia of 4 kilogram metre squared and spins about its axis at an angular speed of 10 radians per second. What is its rotational kinetic energy?
questions.answer: Use the rotational kinetic energy formula: one half times moment of inertia times omega squared. Step 1: square the angular speed: 10 times 10 equals 100. Step 2: multiply by the moment of inertia: 4 times 100 equals 400. Step 3: take one half: one half of 400 equals 200. So the rotational kinetic energy is 200 joules.

questions.q_text: If you double the angular speed of a spinning rigid body while keeping its moment of inertia unchanged, what happens to its rotational kinetic energy?
options: A. It stays the same
B. It doubles
C. It becomes four times as large
D. It becomes half as large

questions.q_text: Explain, starting from a single particle, how we arrive at the result that the total kinetic energy of a rotating rigid body equals one half the moment of inertia times omega squared.
questions.answer: Step 1: Pick any one particle inside the body at a distance (radius) from the axis. Because the body turns with angular speed omega, this particle moves in a circle with linear speed equal to omega times its radius. Step 2: The kinetic energy of that single particle is one half its mass times its speed squared. Substituting speed equals omega times radius gives one half times mass times omega squared times radius squared. Step 3: To get the whole body's energy, add this up over every particle. Since omega is the same for all particles in a rigid body, omega squared can be factored out of the sum. Step 4: What remains inside the sum is each mass multiplied by its radius squared, added over all particles — and that sum is the definition of the moment of inertia. Step 5: Therefore the total kinetic energy is one half times the moment of inertia times omega squared.

questions.q_text: In straight-line motion, power equals force times velocity. What is the rotational equivalent of this expression?
options: A. Torque times angular displacement
B. Torque times angular velocity
C. Moment of inertia times angular velocity
D. Force times angular acceleration

questions.q_text: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, the small amount of work done by a torque over a tiny angular displacement equals which of the following?
options: A. Torque times the small angular displacement
B. Torque times the angular velocity
C. Moment of inertia times the angular displacement
D. Angular acceleration times the angular displacement

questions.q_text: If a constant torque acts on a rotating body as it turns through some total angle, the total work done is equal to what?
options: A. The torque divided by the total angle
B. The torque times the total angle turned
C. One half the torque times the angle squared
D. The torque times the angular velocity squared

questions.q_text: A torque of 8 newton-meters acts on a wheel that is spinning at an angular velocity of 5 radians per second. What power is being delivered to the wheel at that instant?
questions.answer: Power delivered by a torque equals the torque times the angular velocity. Here the torque is 8 newton-meters and the angular velocity is 5 radians per second. Multiplying these together: 8 times 5 equals 40. So the power delivered is 40 watts.

questions.q_text: Explain why the power delivered by a torque can be written as torque times angular velocity, starting from the idea that power is the rate of change of rotational kinetic energy.
questions.answer: Start with the rotational kinetic energy, which is one half times the moment of inertia times the angular velocity squared. Power is the rate at which this energy changes over time. When we look at how this energy changes, the one half and the squared combine so that the rate of change becomes the moment of inertia times the angular velocity times the angular acceleration (the angular acceleration being how fast the angular velocity changes). Now recall that the moment of inertia times the angular acceleration is exactly the definition of torque. So substituting torque in place of moment of inertia times angular acceleration, we get power equals torque times angular velocity. This mirrors the straight-line result that power equals force times velocity, with torque replacing force and angular velocity replacing velocity.

questions.q_text: The moment of inertia of a single particle about a given axis is found by which of the following?
options: A. Its mass multiplied by its distance from the axis
B. Its mass multiplied by the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis
C. The square of its mass multiplied by its distance from the axis
D. Its mass divided by the square of its distance from the axis

questions.q_text: When calculating the moment of inertia of a circular plate (disc) by integration, what is the most convenient shape to choose for the tiny mass element?
options: A. A thin segment along a diameter
B. A small square patch
C. A thin concentric ring
D. A thin hollow spherical shell

questions.q_text: Which statement best describes the 'layering' approach used to find moments of inertia of larger objects?
options: A. A solid sphere is built by stacking thin hollow shells, and a disc is built by stacking thin rings
B. A ring is built from solid spheres
C. A rod is built from spherical shells stacked end to end
D. A disc is built by stacking solid spheres

questions.q_text: For a hollow sphere, why do the three mutually perpendicular axes through its center all give the same moment of inertia?
options: A. Because the sphere has no mass
B. Because the sphere looks the same in every direction (it is symmetric)
C. Because all axes are parallel
D. Because the perpendicular axis theorem only works for flat objects

questions.q_text: Three point masses are fixed to a light rod lying along a straight line. A 2 kilogram mass sits 1 meter from a chosen axis, a 3 kilogram mass sits 2 meters from it, and a 1 kilogram mass sits 3 meters from it, all measured perpendicular to the axis. Find the total moment of inertia about that axis.
questions.answer: We use the definition: moment of inertia is the sum over all particles of mass times the square of perpendicular distance. For the first mass: 2 kilograms times (1 meter) squared = 2 times 1 = 2. For the second mass: 3 kilograms times (2 meters) squared = 3 times 4 = 12. For the third mass: 1 kilogram times (3 meters) squared = 1 times 9 = 9. Now add these contributions together: 2 + 12 + 9 = 23. So the total moment of inertia is 23 kilogram meter squared.

questions.q_text: For a rigid body, about which kind of axis is the moment of inertia always the smallest among a set of parallel axes?
options: A. An axis at the edge of the body
B. An axis passing through the centre of mass
C. An axis far away from the body
D. Any axis perpendicular to the body

questions.q_text: The perpendicular axes theorem can be applied to which type of object?
options: A. Any three-dimensional solid object
B. Only spherical objects
C. Only flat, planar (two-dimensional) bodies
D. Only objects rotating about their centre of mass

questions.q_text: When you move the rotation axis a certain distance away from a parallel axis through the centre of mass, what extra quantity must you add to the moment of inertia?
options: A. The mass times the distance
B. The mass times the square of the distance
C. The mass divided by the distance squared
D. Half the mass times the distance squared

questions.q_text: A thin uniform rod of mass 2 kilograms and length 3 metres has a moment of inertia of 1.5 kilogram metre squared about a perpendicular axis through its centre. Find its moment of inertia about a parallel perpendicular axis passing through one end.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify what we know. Moment of inertia about the centre of mass axis is 1.5 kilogram metre squared. Mass is 2 kilograms. Step 2: Find the distance between the two parallel axes. The centre is at the middle of the rod, and one end is half the length away, so the distance is 3 divided by 2, which is 1.5 metres. Step 3: Apply the parallel axes theorem: moment of inertia about the end equals moment of inertia about the centre plus mass times distance squared. Step 4: Compute the penalty term: 2 times (1.5 squared) equals 2 times 2.25 equals 4.5 kilogram metre squared. Step 5: Add them: 1.5 plus 4.5 equals 6 kilogram metre squared. So the moment of inertia about the end is 6 kilogram metre squared.

questions.q_text: A thin uniform ring lies flat in a plane. Its moment of inertia about an axis perpendicular to its plane through its centre is 8 kilogram metre squared. By symmetry, what is its moment of inertia about a diameter (an axis lying in the plane through the centre)?
questions.answer: Step 1: Use the perpendicular axes theorem. The moment of inertia about the perpendicular (z) axis equals the moment about the x-axis plus the moment about the y-axis, where x and y are two perpendicular diameters in the plane. Step 2: By the symmetry of the ring, both diameters give the same moment of inertia. Call each one I. Then I plus I equals the perpendicular axis value, so 2 times I equals 8. Step 3: Solve for I: I equals 8 divided by 2 equals 4 kilogram metre squared. So the moment of inertia about a diameter is 4 kilogram metre squared.

questions.q_text: What does the radius of gyration of a body represent?
options: A. The actual physical radius of the body
B. The radius of an imaginary ring on which all the mass could be placed to give the same moment of inertia
C. The distance from the centre of mass to the edge
D. The radius at which the body spins fastest

questions.q_text: When analyzing combined rotation and translation from a frame riding with the body, why do we specifically choose the axis through the center of mass?
options: A. Because the center of mass is always the actual axis of rotation seen from the ground
B. Because the pseudo torques about the center of mass add up to exactly zero, so torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration still holds
C. Because the moment of inertia is always smallest about the center of mass
D. Because external forces vanish when measured from the center of mass

questions.q_text: In the strategy for combined motion, how do we describe the total motion of the body?
options: A. As pure translation only, ignoring the spin
B. As pure rotation about a fixed ground axis
C. As the spinning part (in the moving frame) plus the motion of that frame
D. As the difference between rotation and translation

questions.q_text: Why is the frame that rides along with a rolling body generally a noninertial frame?
options: A. Because the body is spinning at constant speed
B. Because the center of mass of the body is usually accelerating
C. Because there are no external forces acting
D. Because the frame is at rest relative to the ground

questions.q_text: A solid object of total mass 4 kilograms experiences two external forces in the plane of motion: one of 12 newtons pointing east, and another of 4 newtons pointing west. Find the acceleration of the center of mass.
questions.answer: Step 1: Add the external forces as vectors. Taking east as positive, the net force is 12 newtons minus 4 newtons, which equals 8 newtons pointing east. Step 2: Divide the net force by the total mass to get the acceleration of the center of mass. That is 8 newtons divided by 4 kilograms, which equals 2 meters per second squared. Step 3: State the direction. The acceleration of the center of mass is 2 meters per second squared pointing east.

questions.q_text: A disc has a moment of inertia of 0.5 kilogram meter squared about a line through its center of mass perpendicular to its plane. The total external torque about that same line is 3 newton meters. Find the angular acceleration about the center of mass.
questions.answer: Step 1: Use the rule that survives about the center of mass: torque equals moment of inertia times angular acceleration. Step 2: Rearrange to solve for angular acceleration: angular acceleration equals torque divided by moment of inertia. Step 3: Substitute the values: 3 newton meters divided by 0.5 kilogram meter squared equals 6 radians per second squared. So the angular acceleration about the center of mass is 6 radians per second squared.

questions.q_text: The pseudo torques vanish about the center of mass because of which fact?
options: A. The sum of mass times position measured from the center of mass is zero
B. The total external force is always zero
C. The body is rigid
D. Pseudo forces never act on rotating bodies

questions.q_text: A wheel is rolling without slipping, and the centre of the wheel moves forward at 4 metres per second. What is the speed of the topmost point of the wheel?
options: A. 0 metres per second
B. 2 metres per second
C. 4 metres per second
D. 8 metres per second

questions.q_text: During pure rolling, what is special about the point of the wheel that is touching the ground at any given instant?
options: A. It moves at the same speed as the centre
B. Its velocity is momentarily zero
C. It moves backward relative to the ground
D. It moves twice as fast as the centre

questions.q_text: You slam the brakes on a wet road and the wheel slides forward while barely spinning. How does the centre's speed compare to the radius times the angular velocity?
options: A. The centre moves slower than radius times angular velocity
B. The centre moves faster than radius times angular velocity
C. They are exactly equal
D. The centre does not move at all

questions.q_text: A bicycle wheel has a radius of 0.35 metres and is rolling without slipping. How far forward does the bicycle travel during one complete rotation of the wheel? Use pi as approximately 3.14.
questions.answer: In pure rolling, one complete rotation moves the wheel forward by a distance equal to its circumference. The circumference equals two times pi times the radius. So we compute two times 3.14 times 0.35. First, two times 3.14 equals 6.28. Then 6.28 times 0.35 equals 2.198. Therefore the bicycle travels about 2.20 metres in one full rotation.

questions.q_text: A wheel of radius 0.5 metres rolls without slipping with an angular velocity of 10 radians per second. Find the speed of the centre and the speed of the topmost point.
questions.answer: For pure rolling, the speed of the centre equals the radius times the angular velocity. So the centre's speed is 0.5 times 10, which equals 5 metres per second. The topmost point moves at twice the centre's speed in pure rolling, so it moves at 2 times 5, which equals 10 metres per second. The bottom contact point, for completeness, has zero velocity at that instant.

questions.q_text: A car wheel stuck in mud spins very fast but the car barely moves forward. This is an example of:
options: A. Pure rolling
B. Forward slipping, with the contact point rubbing forward
C. Backward slipping, with the contact point rubbing backward
D. Pure straight-line motion with no spin

questions.q_text: When we derive the kinetic energy of a body that is both rotating and translating, a cross term appears when we square each particle's velocity. Why does this cross term disappear?
options: A. Because the moment of inertia about the center of mass is always zero
B. Because the velocity of the center of mass measured in the center-of-mass frame is zero
C. Because the angular velocity is assumed to be very small
D. Because friction at the contact point cancels it out

questions.q_text: For a body undergoing combined rotation and translation, the total kinetic energy is the sum of which two pieces?
options: A. Rotational energy about the contact point plus translational energy of the center of mass
B. Rotational energy about the center of mass plus translational energy of the center of mass
C. Translational energy of every particle plus the potential energy
D. Rotational energy about the center of mass plus rotational energy about the contact point

questions.q_text: In pure rolling without slipping, the kinetic energy can be written as one half times the moment of inertia about the contact point times the angular velocity squared. What does this tell us physically about the rolling body at any instant?
options: A. The body is purely translating with no rotation
B. The body behaves as if purely rotating about the contact point with the ground
C. The body has no kinetic energy at the contact point
D. The contact point moves faster than the center of mass

questions.q_text: A uniform disc of mass 2 kilograms and radius 0.1 meters rolls without slipping with its center moving at 3 meters per second. The moment of inertia of a disc about its center is one half times mass times radius squared. Find the translational kinetic energy, the rotational kinetic energy, and the total kinetic energy.
questions.answer:
Step 1: Translational kinetic energy. This is one half times mass times the speed of the center squared. That is one half times 2 times 3 squared, which is one half times 2 times 9, giving 9 joules.

Step 2: Find the angular velocity. For rolling without slipping, the center's speed equals radius times angular velocity, so angular velocity equals speed divided by radius, which is 3 divided by 0.1, giving 30 radians per second.

Step 3: Moment of inertia about the center. This is one half times mass times radius squared, which is one half times 2 times 0.1 squared. That is one half times 2 times 0.01, giving 0.01 kilogram meter squared.

Step 4: Rotational kinetic energy. This is one half times moment of inertia times angular velocity squared, which is one half times 0.01 times 30 squared. That is one half times 0.01 times 900, giving 4.5 joules.

Step 5: Total kinetic energy. Add the two pieces: 9 plus 4.5 equals 13.5 joules.

questions.q_text: Using the same disc as before (mass 2 kilograms, radius 0.1 meters, angular velocity 30 radians per second), compute the kinetic energy directly as one half times the moment of inertia about the contact point times the angular velocity squared, and confirm it matches the total found earlier. Use the parallel axis theorem.
questions.answer:
Step 1: Moment of inertia about the center is one half times mass times radius squared, which is one half times 2 times 0.01, giving 0.01 kilogram meter squared.

Step 2: Apply the parallel axis theorem. The contact point is a distance equal to the radius from the center, so we add mass times radius squared. That is 2 times 0.01, giving 0.02 kilogram meter squared. The total moment of inertia about the contact point is 0.01 plus 0.02, equal to 0.03 kilogram meter squared.

Step 3: Kinetic energy is one half times moment of inertia about contact point times angular velocity squared. That is one half times 0.03 times 30 squared, which is one half times 0.03 times 900. That gives one half times 27, equal to 13.5 joules.

Step 4: This matches the total kinetic energy of 13.5 joules found from the rotation-plus-translation method, confirming both viewpoints give the same answer.

questions.q_text: When we split the total angular momentum of a spinning, moving body about a point O, two terms vanish and two survive. What are the two terms that survive?
options: A. The spin about the center of mass, plus the whole mass treated as a point at the center of mass moving about O
B. The spin about O, plus the translation about the center of mass
C. Two cross terms involving position relative to O and velocity relative to the center of mass
D. The kinetic energy of spinning, plus the kinetic energy of translation

questions.q_text: Why do two of the four terms in the angular momentum expansion vanish?
options: A. Because the body is rigid and cannot deform
B. Because the sum of mass times position, and mass times velocity, measured from the center of mass, are each zero
C. Because the point O is chosen to lie on the center of mass
D. Because the angular velocity of the body is constant

questions.q_text: The first surviving term, the angular momentum about the center of mass, represents what an observer would see if they were doing what?
options: A. Standing fixed at the point O
B. Riding along with the center of mass and watching only the spinning
C. Moving faster than the center of mass
D. Located at the edge of the rolling wheel

questions.q_text: Consider a wheel spinning in place about its own center, with its center of mass not moving at all. What is its total angular momentum about an external point O?
options: A. Zero, because the center of mass is not moving
B. Only the travel term, since spinning does not count
C. Only the spin term about the center of mass, since the travel term is zero
D. The spin term plus the travel term, both nonzero

questions.q_text: A uniform disk of mass 4 kilograms and radius 0.5 meters rolls so that its center of mass moves in a straight line at 3 meters per second. The disk also spins so that its angular momentum about its own center is 3 kilogram meter squared per second. The center of mass passes a fixed point O at a perpendicular distance of 2 meters from O's line of sight to the motion. Find the total angular momentum of the disk about O at that instant.
questions.answer: The total angular momentum is the spin part plus the travel part. Step 1: The spin part is the angular momentum about the center of mass, given as 3 kilogram meter squared per second. Step 2: The travel part treats the whole mass as a point at the center of mass. Its magnitude is mass times center-of-mass speed times the perpendicular distance from O. That is 4 kilograms times 3 meters per second times 2 meters, which equals 24 kilogram meter squared per second. Step 3: Add them together: 3 plus 24 equals 27 kilogram meter squared per second. So the total angular momentum of the disk about O is 27 kilogram meter squared per second.

questions.q_text: Two students compute the travel term (the whole mass treated as a point at the center of mass) about two different fixed points. The center of mass moves at the same velocity. What determines whether their travel terms differ?
options: A. They are always equal regardless of the chosen point
B. They differ if the perpendicular distances from the two points to the line of motion differ
C. They differ only if the body's spin changes
D. They differ only if the mass of the body changes

questions.q_text: If we model the rolling sphere as touching the table at a single perfect point, what problem arises with using friction alone to explain why it stops?
options: A. Friction would push the sphere upward off the table
B. The backward friction at the bottom creates a torque that would speed up the spinning, not slow it
C. Friction would have to act in the same direction as the motion
D. Friction would have no effect on the forward motion at all

questions.q_text: Why does the normal force end up acting in front of the sphere's center rather than straight up through it?
options: A. The weight of the sphere pulls it forward
B. Friction physically drags the normal force forward
C. The front part of the small contact area presses against the table more strongly than the back part
D. The table tilts slightly downward in the direction of motion

questions.q_text: In the full explanation, which force is responsible for slowing the forward motion of the center, and which is responsible for slowing the rotation?
options: A. Friction slows the forward motion; the shifted normal force slows the rotation
B. The shifted normal force slows the forward motion; friction slows the rotation
C. Weight slows the forward motion; friction slows the rotation
D. Friction slows both the forward motion and the rotation

questions.q_text: What is the central lesson about the idealized 'single contact point' assumption in this explanation?
options: A. It is exactly correct and surfaces never deform
B. It is just an approximation; real surfaces deform and contact spreads out over a small area
C. It applies only to spheres made of metal
D. It means rolling objects should roll forever

questions.q_text: Explain step by step why a sphere rolling on a table eventually stops, identifying each force and the torque it produces.
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the forces. Three forces act on the sphere: its weight pulling straight down, the normal force from the table pushing up, and friction at the contact region. Step 2: Consider friction. As the center of the sphere slows, friction points backward, opposite to the direction of motion, which correctly slows the forward translation. Step 3: Spot the problem. That backward friction acts at the bottom of the sphere, so it creates a torque that tends to make the ball roll more — speeding up the spin rather than slowing it. So friction alone cannot stop the rotation; we need an opposing (anticlockwise) torque. Step 4: Find the missing torque. In reality the sphere and table deform slightly near contact, so they touch over a small area instead of a single point. The front of this area presses harder than the back, which shifts the effective normal force forward of the center. Step 5: Conclude. Because the normal force no longer passes through the center, it produces an anticlockwise torque that slows the rotation. Thus friction slows the center's forward motion while the forward-shifted normal force slows the spinning, and together they bring the sphere to rest. This deformation effect is called rolling friction, and it is why nothing rolls forever.
